domains.title: Great-power conflict, war, and geopolitical order

research.domain: Great-power conflict, war, and geopolitical order
research.state_of_play:
As of late July 2026 the international system has visibly shifted from "contested but rule-bound" toward openly coercive unilateralism, and H1 2026 delivered three discontinuities I verified by search.

(1) The United States used force twice at a scale not seen since 2003. On 3 January 2026, ~200 US special operations forces conducted Operation Absolute Resolve in Caracas, capturing Nicolas Maduro; Delcy Rodriguez was sworn in as interim president on 5 January, with Trump saying the US would "run the country" through a transition. Condemnation came mostly from Latin America, Africa and Asia; most NATO states backed it. Then on 28 February 2026 the US and Israel launched roughly 900 strikes in 12 hours across Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and much of the senior military leadership. Mojtaba Khamenei assumed the leadership amid what analysts describe as unprecedented institutional friction; June 2026 saw open elite splits (the 30 June state-TV censoring of Speaker Ghalibaf), strikes and protests across Tehran, Gilan and Kurdistan, and rising armed attacks on regime forces. Iran retaliated against US embassies, bases and Gulf oil infrastructure and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in March (Brent broke $100; one analyst publicly modelled $150-200). A Pakistan-mediated two-week ceasefire on 8 April was extended indefinitely on 21 April; a 14 June MoU was meant to formally end the war within 60 days. It failed: in July Iran struck three commercial vessels deviating from its pre-approved corridor, the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports from 14 July plus a 20% fee on Hormuz cargo (Brent +9.5% to >$83, later $85.87 then -11.3%), and the Houthis declared the Saudi détente over and blockaded Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb. On 27 July CNN reported the US paused new strikes while Iran denied any negotiations. IAEA monitoring of Iran remains near-totally lost since mid-2025; breakout estimates range absurdly widely (days, 9-12 months per US IC, ~2.5 years accounting for strike damage), and Iranian legislation to reconsider NPT membership is live.

(2) Arms control ended. New START expired 4-5 February 2026 with no successor and no negotiation underway — the first time since ~1972 that no legally binding cap constrains US and Russian strategic forces. Meanwhile Golden Dome moved from concept to contracts (12 firms selected for space-based interceptors in April 2026; $185bn official, ~$1.2T/20yr independent estimates), which Beijing calls "strongly offensive." North Korea's Kim inspected a new weapons-grade fissile material plant in June 2026 and promised "exponential" expansion; the test site is postured but no seventh test has occurred. Proliferation debate is mainstream in Seoul (75-80% public support), Warsaw (President Nawrocki backed an independent deterrent in February) and, more tentatively, Tokyo.

(3) The transatlantic bargain is being renegotiated under stress. The NATO Ankara summit (7-8 July 2026) reaffirmed 5% GDP by 2035 (3.5% core) and announced >$50bn in procurement; European allies and Canada added $139bn in core defence in 2025. Simultaneously a six-month US Europe Posture Review formally began 28 July 2026, with fighters cut ~150→100, ISR 26→15, eight tankers withdrawn and ~5,000 troops leaving Germany — explicitly abandoning tripwire logic for "NATO 3.0." Baltic and Polish leaders warned in mid-July that Russia may stage limited hybrid or drone provocations, possibly using captured Ukrainian drones.

Ukraine: the war continues. Russian gains collapsed from 2,190 km² (Jan-Jun 2025) to 623 km² (Jan-Jun 2026); Pokrovsk-Kostiantynivka remains the main effort with infiltration rather than consolidation. Russian monthly casualties (>30k) now exceed recruitment (~27k), with cumulative permanent losses assessed at ~1.2M by Dutch MIVD. Only short truces (Easter, 11 April; Victory Day, 9-11 May) have held; Trump and Zelensky met at Ankara on 8 July to rework the negotiating framework, and Ukrainian officials publicly favour a partial ceasefire as most realistic. The EU's 21st package (23 July) froze the oil price cap at $44.10/bbl to July 2027 and hit LNG for the first time.

Not verified this session, relying on pre-2026 knowledge: precise 2025-26 Taiwan ADIZ sortie totals, current IMF COFER reserve shares, UCDP 2025 conflict counts, and India-Pakistan post-2025 force posture details.

scheduled_events.name: Deadline from 14 June US-Iran MoU to formally end the 2026 Iran war (60 days)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Failure already partly realised via July strikes/blockade; a formal collapse re-prices Hormuz risk and Gulf insurance.

scheduled_events.name: 18th BRICS Summit, New Delhi (India presidency)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Tests whether de-dollarization moves from rhetoric to plumbing (BRICS Pay, gold-linked Unit, CBDC interoperability) or is again shelved by India.

scheduled_events.name: US midterm elections
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Determines congressional constraint on unilateral force use (Venezuela, Iran), Ukraine funding, and NATO drawdown politics.

scheduled_events.name: Expiry of the US-China tariff truce agreed at Busan
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: If it lapses, rare-earth export controls and tech restrictions resume, raising the economic-coercion baseline around Taiwan.

scheduled_events.name: Results of the six-month US Europe Force Posture Review
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Sets the actual size of the US conventional commitment to NATO's eastern flank and therefore Article 5 credibility.

scheduled_events.name: French presidential election
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: A nationalist-right presidency would reshape EU sanctions unanimity, Ukraine aid, and the future of French extended deterrence talk.

scheduled_events.name: PLA 100th anniversary and Xi's 2027 capability milestone
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Widely used as the benchmark date for PLA 'capability to take Taiwan'; watch it as capability, not intent.

scheduled_events.name: 21st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Xi's succession signalling and the post-purge PLA leadership slate set the risk-appetite of the next five years.

scheduled_events.name: Taiwan presidential and legislative elections
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: A third DPP term or a KMT restoration is the single largest swing factor in cross-Strait coercion levels for 2028-2032.

scheduled_events.name: US presidential election
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Decides whether the 2025-2028 unilateralist doctrine (regime-decapitation strikes, blockades, burden-shifting) is institutionalised or reversed.

scheduled_events.name: NATO scheduled review of the 5%-of-GDP pledge
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First formal checkpoint on whether Europe is actually funding the conventional-defence handover.

scheduled_events.name: Iranian presidential election
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First scheduled national vote after the Khamenei succession; a legitimacy stress test for the post-2026 order in Tehran.

scheduled_events.name: Russian presidential election
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Putin would be 77; the succession question is the largest single discontinuity risk for the Russia-Ukraine and Russia-NATO tracks.

scheduled_events.name: South Korean presidential election
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: With 75-80% public support for indigenous nuclear weapons, a pro-nuclear candidate would be the most likely proliferation trigger of the decade.

scheduled_events.name: EU/G7 Russian oil price cap freeze expires
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Reopens the dynamic-mechanism fight that nearly raised the cap to ~$58 during the Hormuz shock.

discrete_risks.name: Durable Russia-Ukraine ceasefire (>=180 consecutive days)
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A ceasefire covering the entire land front between Russian and Ukrainian forces holds for at least 180 consecutive days without resumption of sustained offensive ground operations or systematic long-range strikes on cities, as assessed by ISW/OSCE-successor monitoring or equivalent consensus reporting. Short holiday truces (e.g. April/May 2026) do NOT count.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Russian gains collapsed 72% year-on-year (623 km2 Jan-Jun 2026 vs 2190 km2 in 2025) while monthly casualties (>30k) now exceed recruitment (~27k) and Moscow has blown through its 2026 deficit allowance and is selling gold. Ukraine's leadership publicly says a partial ceasefire is the realistic outcome. Trump met Zelensky at Ankara on 8 July to rework the framework, and Washington is simultaneously drawing down in Europe, which raises its incentive to close the file. The blockers are territorial recognition and monitoring, not battlefield capacity.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Interstate wars lasting >4 years: of the ~15 such conflicts since 1945 (Iran-Iraq, Ethiopia-Eritrea, Vietnam, etc.), most terminated within 2-4 years of the point where one side's attrition exceeded replacement. Median remaining duration once mutual exhaustion is documented is roughly 18-30 months, implying ~40-55% within 18 months.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Putin has repeatedly preferred continued war to any settlement that does not deliver the four annexed oblasts, and 2026 attrition has not produced Ukrainian collapse or Russian regime stress sufficient to change that. The 2026 truces were theatrical, not preparatory. A US drawdown may reduce rather than increase Moscow's urgency to settle: if Washington is leaving anyway, waiting is cheap. I could easily be 15 points too high at 2027.

discrete_risks.name: Strait of Hormuz crude transit below 50% of 2025 baseline for >=30 consecutive days (new episode after 1 Aug 2026)
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Crude-plus-condensate transit through Hormuz, per EIA/Vortexa/Kpler monthly data, falls below 50% of the 2025 monthly average for at least 30 consecutive days, in an episode beginning on or after 1 August 2026.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is close to the current state rather than a tail: Iran effectively shut the strait in March 2026, the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July with a 20% cargo fee, 24 tankers are queued at Kharg, the Houthis have blockaded Saudi-linked Bab el-Mandeb traffic, and talks are stalled (US paused strikes 27 July; Iran denies negotiations). Mines, insurance withdrawal and war-risk premia produce closure-equivalent flow collapse even without a formal Iranian declaration.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Hormuz has never been fully closed in 60 years despite the 1984-88 Tanker War (~450 ships hit, flows down but not halted) and 2019 limpet-mine attacks. Unconditional base rate of a 30-day >50% flow collapse is ~1-2%/yr. The conditional rate given an active US-Iran shooting war and an existing blockade is an order of magnitude higher.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Iran's own export revenue and China's crude supply both run through Hormuz, so Tehran's rational play is harassment that raises prices without stopping flow, and the March-April episode ended within weeks precisely for that reason. Markets are pricing normalisation (Brent fell back toward $70 in late June). If Washington accepts a corridor arrangement, flows normalise fast and I am 25 points too high.

discrete_risks.name: North Korea conducts a seventh nuclear explosive test
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A nuclear explosive test on DPRK territory confirmed by CTBTO seismic/radionuclide detection or by US/ROK/Japanese government statement.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Punggye-ri has been restored and DIA assesses Pyongyang is postured to test at a time of its choosing. Kim inspected a new weapons-grade fissile material plant in June 2026 and announced 'exponential' expansion, having doubled production capacity in five years. The Hwasong-20 solid ICBM (unveiled Oct 2025) is not yet flight-tested. With New START dead and US-DPRK diplomacy dormant, the Chinese restraint that has plausibly deterred a test since 2017 is the main remaining brake, and Beijing's incentive to restrain Pyongyang falls as US-China competition hardens.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Six tests in 2006, 2009, 2013, 2016 (x2), 2017 — six events in 20 years = ~30%/yr during the active period, but zero in the nine years since. A regime-switching model with an ~8%/yr hazard in the current 'postured but restrained' state fits the observed drought.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Nine years of restraint is a lot of evidence. Kim gets the deterrence benefit from missile tests at far lower diplomatic cost, values his warming ties with Moscow (which does not want a test), and depends on Chinese trade. Warhead miniaturisation may simply no longer require explosive validation. A flat 3%/yr would give ~15% by 2031, and that view is defensible.

discrete_risks.name: A state that does not now possess nuclear weapons tests a device or is confirmed to possess one
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Any state other than the US, Russia, UK, France, China, India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea either (a) conducts a nuclear explosive test, (b) officially declares possession of an assembled nuclear weapon, or (c) is assessed by the IAEA or by the US intelligence community in a public statement to possess one.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Four simultaneous demand shocks: New START's expiry (Feb 2026) removed the last visible restraint norm; the US is visibly burden-shifting in Europe (posture review begun 28 July 2026) and used decapitating force against a non-nuclear state (Iran, Feb 2026), which is the cleanest possible lesson in the value of a deterrent; ROK public support for the bomb runs 75-80%; Poland's president endorsed an independent deterrent in Feb 2026; Iran's monitoring has collapsed and NPT-withdrawal legislation is live. Iran is the most likely single candidate, then ROK.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: New nuclear-weapon states: 1945, 1949, 1952, 1960, 1964, 1974, ~1979 (Israel earlier), 1998 (x2), 2006. That is 10 in 81 years, ~0.12/yr unconditional, and only one in the last 28 years (~0.036/yr). I am pricing roughly 3-4x the recent base rate.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The nonproliferation record is far more robust than nuclear-crisis commentary implies: dozens of states have had latent capability for decades and abstained, and every serious ROK/Japan analysis concludes the alliance, export-control and sanctions costs still dominate. Iran's programme has just been physically wrecked and its leadership decapitated, which delays rather than accelerates. Weaponisation is a decision with years of observable lead time; nothing observable has crossed that line.

discrete_risks.name: Iran tests or is confirmed to possess an assembled nuclear weapon
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Iran conducts a nuclear explosive test, publicly declares possession, or is publicly assessed by the IAEA or the US intelligence community to possess at least one assembled nuclear weapon.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Motive is at a historic maximum — the Supreme Leader was killed by an air campaign, the state has been blockaded, and NPT-withdrawal legislation is before the Majlis — but capability was heavily degraded by the June 2025 and February 2026 campaigns, and IAEA monitoring loss cuts both ways (it hides progress but also removes the safety of a declared programme). Serious assessments diverge from 'weeks' to 'at least 2.5 years absent foreign assistance'; the latter accounts for centrifuge, conversion and metallurgy destruction and is more credible. Any detected dash likely triggers another US-Israeli campaign, which is itself a large suppressant.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: States that began a weapons dash while under active military attack and comprehensive sanctions: Iraq 1981-91 (failed), Syria 2007 (destroyed), Libya 2003 (abandoned), DPRK 1994-2006 (succeeded, but with no ongoing bombardment). Roughly 1 success in 4-5 attempts, over 10-15 year timescales.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The strongest counter is that Iran may already have diverted the 440.9 kg of 60% HEU to undeclared sites before February 2026 and that with no inspectors, a crude device could be assembled far faster than public estimates — in which case my 2027 number is several times too low. The opposite contrarian case is that a regime fighting for internal survival prioritises regime security over a programme that provably invites annihilation.

discrete_risks.name: PRC imposes a declared and enforced quarantine or blockade of Taiwan lasting >=7 days
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: PRC state organs (PLA, Coast Guard or maritime authorities) publicly declare a quarantine, inspection regime or blockade of Taiwan's ports/airspace AND enforce it by boarding, turning back or interdicting at least ten commercial vessels or aircraft, sustained for at least seven consecutive days.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The PLA has rehearsed the components repeatedly (encirclement exercises, coast guard 'law-enforcement' patrols, drone swarm development) and quarantine is the option that maximises coercive effect while minimising the chance of triggering a US shooting response. But ODNI's March 2026 Annual Threat Assessment states Chinese leaders lack a fixed timeline and are not planning an invasion in 2027, and Beijing spent H1 2026 stabilising the US relationship (Trump-Xi Beijing summit 15 May, $17bn/yr agricultural purchases, 200 Boeing aircraft, tariff truce to Nov 2026). Economic conditions in China argue for postponement. The Jan-2028 Taiwan election is the more natural forcing point.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Peacetime naval quarantines of a functioning state's ports by a great power: Cuba 1962, Berlin 1948-49 (land), limited Israeli/Gaza cases. Roughly 2-3 clear instances in 80 years of great-power practice — under 4%/yr even in tense dyads, and Beijing has never done it despite 30 years of Taiwan crises.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Quarantine is cheap, reversible and hard to answer, and Beijing may read the Venezuela and Iran operations as proof that unilateral coercion now goes unpunished. Japan's Takaichi has explicitly said a blockade could be a 'survival-threatening situation' triggering JSDF action, which raises the stakes and could make Beijing want to establish the precedent early, while the US is distracted in the Gulf. A 2031 figure of 25% is defensible.

discrete_risks.name: PRC launches an amphibious or airborne assault on Taiwan's main island
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: PLA forces conduct an opposed landing or airborne insertion on Taiwan proper (not offshore islands) involving at least 1,000 personnel, confirmed by Taiwan MND or US government statement.
discrete_risks.reasoning: An opposed landing across 130 km against a prepared defender, with Japan signalling intervention and US carriers within range, remains the hardest military operation in the world; ODNI (March 2026) assesses no invasion plan for 2027. The PLA is mid-purge of senior officers and just raised its budget only 7% (1.91tn yuan / $277bn), slightly below the 7.2% of the prior three years — not a mobilisation signature. Capability milestones (Sichuan LHA commissioning, SLBM demonstration in the South Pacific) are real but are about deterrence and far-seas presence, not D-Day.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Large opposed amphibious invasions since 1950: Inchon (1950), Suez (1956), Bay of Pigs (1961), Falklands (1982), Grenada (1983). Five in 76 years globally, of which zero against a defender with modern anti-ship missiles and an allied great-power guarantor. Unconditional base rate well under 1%/yr for any given dyad.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Polymarket implies ~2.5% by 30 Sep 2026 and ~14.5% by end-2027, which if taken at face value is far above my numbers; longshot bias explains most but perhaps not all of that gap. If Beijing concludes the US is genuinely disengaging (Europe posture review, Gulf entanglement, midterm chaos) and that its own economic trajectory is deteriorating, a use-it-or-lose-it logic could compress the timeline sharply.

discrete_risks.name: NATO invokes Article 5 in response to a Russian attack
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The North Atlantic Council formally invokes Article 5 of the Washington Treaty citing an armed attack attributable to Russia or Belarus.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Baltic and Polish leaders warned in mid-July 2026 that Russia is planning limited hybrid or military provocations, potentially using captured Ukrainian drones for deniable or false-flag strikes; Sandworm already wipered Polish energy infrastructure in Dec 2025 (~30 sites, a plant serving 500,000 customers). The design of these operations is precisely to stay below Article 5, and NATO's revealed preference through 2024-2026 (drone incursions, cable cuts, sabotage, assassination plots) has been Article 4 consultations, never Article 5. A Ukraine settlement would free Russian forces but also reduce the pretext; the US drawdown cuts both ways.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Article 5 has been invoked once in 77 years (September 2001, and not against a state). Article 4 has been invoked ~8 times. Unconditional rate ~1.3%/yr; conditional on the most confrontational Russia-NATO period since 1983, I use roughly 2%/yr declining if Ukraine settles.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Deniable hybrid attacks are cumulative: at some point a Polish or Lithuanian government facing mass-casualty sabotage will demand Article 5 rather than Article 4, and allies unwilling to fight would then face a credibility crisis they might prefer to resolve by invoking and responding narrowly. Also, a formal invocation does not require war — it could be invoked for a limited response, which makes it cheaper and thus more likely than the 'means war' framing implies.

discrete_risks.name: Direct US-PRC military exchange causing at least one fatality
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: An exchange of fire (kinetic, including missile, air, naval or ground fire) between US and PLA/PAP/China Coast Guard forces resulting in at least one death on either side, acknowledged by either government or confirmed by credible multi-source reporting.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Unsafe intercepts and South China Sea coast guard aggression against Philippine vessels (a US treaty ally) are the main pathways; a fatal collision or water-cannon death involving US personnel or a US-escorted convoy is more likely than a deliberate engagement. H1 2026 actually moved the wrong way for this risk in the good sense — the 15 May Beijing summit produced trade boards and purchase commitments, and both sides want the Nov 2026 tariff truce extended.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: US-PRC lethal incidents since 1979: none (the 2001 EP-3 collision killed a Chinese pilot but was not an exchange of fire; Belgrade 1999 was a strike on an embassy, not a force-on-force clash). Roughly 0-1 in 47 years of near-continuous contact.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The Philippines is the weak link: Manila has a mutual defence treaty, Chinese coast guard tactics have already caused serious injuries at Second Thomas Shoal, and Washington has repeatedly said the treaty covers armed attacks on Philippine public vessels. One death changes the political physics instantly. Arguably 2027 should be 6-8%.

discrete_risks.name: Lethal armed clash between Chinese and Japanese state forces
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: An exchange of fire or deliberate ramming between PLA/CCG and JSDF/JCG units resulting in at least one death, confirmed by either government.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Japan-China relations entered a deep freeze after PM Takaichi's November 2025 statement that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could be a 'survival-threatening situation' permitting JSDF action. Beijing has responded with seafood bans, travel warnings, sustained gray-zone harassment around the Senkakus and courting of Japanese opposition parties. Japan is revising its three security documents in 2026, easing arms export rules and selling Mogami frigates to Australia. Contact frequency around the Senkakus is at historic highs, and China now runs armed coast guard cutters there routinely.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Zero lethal PRC-Japan state-force incidents since 1945, across 15 years of intensive Senkaku contact (2010-2026) including the 2010 trawler collision and 2012-13 fire-control radar lock-on. Unconditional rate near 0.5%/yr; I roughly triple it for the current freeze.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Both militaries are highly professional, a maritime-air liaison hotline exists since 2018, and Beijing's coercion toolkit against Japan is deliberately economic precisely to avoid this. Equally, the contrarian case in the other direction: Chinese fishing-militia swarms are not professional, and a single death from a ramming would be much harder to de-escalate than commentators assume.

discrete_risks.name: India-Pakistan fighting causing >=1,000 combined battle deaths in 12 months
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Direct state-on-state armed conflict between Indian and Pakistani forces producing at least 1,000 combined military and civilian deaths within any rolling 12-month period, per UCDP or ACLED coding.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The May 2025 exchange established a new and more dangerous equilibrium: India has normalised deep conventional strikes as the response to mass-casualty terrorism, the Indus Waters Treaty is in abeyance, and the 2025 ceasefire is fragile with mutual violation claims. Crisis Group's 'armed coexistence with little room for diplomacy' is the right frame. The trigger is exogenous — a jihadist attack in India — and the escalation ladder is now shorter than it was pre-2019. Pakistan's simultaneous emergence as a US-favoured mediator (it brokered the April 2026 Iran ceasefire) modestly raises Washington's ability to cap crises.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Indo-Pak conflicts exceeding 1,000 deaths: 1947-48, 1965, 1971, 1999 (Kargil, ~1,000-1,300). Four in 79 years = ~5%/yr, but three of four occurred pre-1972 before both went nuclear; post-1998 the rate is ~1 in 28 years (~3.5%/yr) with an intensified 2016/2019/2025 pattern of sub-threshold strikes.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Every post-1998 crisis has terminated within days at well under 1,000 deaths precisely because nuclear weapons work as advertised, and outside mediation (US, Gulf states) reliably materialises within 72 hours. The 2025 episode confirmed rather than broke this. A 3%/yr flat rate giving ~10% by 2031 is entirely defensible.

discrete_risks.name: A nuclear weapon is detonated in an act of war or hostility anywhere in the world
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A nuclear explosive device is detonated with hostile intent against a state, non-state actor or territory (excluding tests, accidents and demonstration detonations over unpopulated own territory), confirmed by the detonating state or by CTBTO/national technical means.
discrete_risks.reasoning: No treaty caps US and Russian forces for the first time since 1972, four nuclear dyads (US-Russia, India-Pakistan, US-DPRK, US-China) are simultaneously stressed, and the norm against decapitating a nuclear-threshold state's leadership was just broken. Against that, forecasters have consistently and correctly priced these events very low; Metaculus rated Russian use in Ukraine at ~0.1% even at the war's most acute moments, and superforecasters put nuclear catastrophe by 2045 at ~1%. I sit deliberately between the superforecaster (~1%) and domain-expert (~5%) anchors for a ~10-year horizon.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: One instance (August 1945, two devices) in 81 years of nuclear weapons existing = ~1.2%/yr counted naively, but zero in the 81 years since = an upper bound of roughly 0.4%/yr at 90% confidence given no repeat. I use ~0.5%/yr rising slowly.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The honest contrarian case is that this number is unknowable and my precision is fake. The specific upward argument: tactical use by a losing conventional power (Russia against a NATO intervention, Pakistan against an Indian armoured thrust, DPRK against an ROK/US advance) has non-trivial doctrinal support in all three cases, and none of those doctrines have ever been tested. The downward argument: 81 years of crises, including Cuba, Able Archer and 2022, produced zero use.

discrete_risks.name: New US-Russia agreement capping deployed strategic nuclear warheads
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The US and Russia sign a bilateral agreement (treaty, executive agreement, or formal reciprocal political commitment announced by both heads of state) that establishes a numerical ceiling on deployed strategic nuclear warheads or delivery vehicles.
discrete_risks.reasoning: New START lapsed on 4-5 February 2026 with no negotiation underway. The two structural obstacles are Golden Dome (Moscow will demand missile-defence limits Washington will not concede, having just contracted 12 firms for space-based interceptors) and China's build-up (Washington wants trilateral limits Beijing rejects). A Ukraine settlement is a near-necessary precondition, which is why my 2031 number is much higher than 2027. Both sides have short-run fiscal reasons to avoid an uncapped race.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: US-Russia/Soviet strategic arms agreements: SALT I (1972), SALT II (1979), START I (1991), START II (1993), SORT (2002), New START (2010) — six in 54 years, roughly one per nine years, but every one was negotiated during a period of at least minimal detente. Zero were concluded during an active proxy war.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Trump has repeatedly expressed personal interest in denuclearisation deals and likes signable bilateral summits, and both arsenals are expensive to expand; a headline-friendly warhead ceiling with weak verification is exactly the kind of agreement this administration might produce quickly. My 2027 number could be double. Conversely, a politically binding commitment without verification may be worth so little that scoring it 'yes' overstates the change.

discrete_risks.name: State-attributed cyberattack causing >=24h electricity loss to >=1 million people in a NATO or OECD country
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A cyberattack publicly attributed by the victim government or by the EU/NATO to a state or state-sponsored actor causes loss of electrical supply to at least one million people for at least 24 consecutive hours in a NATO or OECD member state.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Capability is demonstrated and pre-positioning is confirmed: Sandworm deployed DynoWiper against ~30 Polish energy sites in December 2025 including a plant serving ~500,000 heat customers; the EU attributed sabotage and cyberespionage against European defence industry and critical infrastructure to FSB Center 16; CISA warned on 8 April 2026 that Iran-linked actors disrupted US PLCs in grid operations; Volt Typhoon remains embedded in US energy IT/OT. What is missing is not capability but the decision to cross a threshold that invites kinetic retaliation — which is exactly what a Russia-NATO confrontation or an Iran endgame could supply.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Confirmed cyber-caused blackouts ever: Ukraine December 2015 (~230,000 customers, ~6 hours) and December 2016 (Kyiv, ~1 hour). Two events in 11 years, both an order of magnitude below the 1-million-for-24-hours threshold, and neither in a NATO state. Unconditional rate for the specified threshold is well under 1%/yr.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Grid attacks at this scale are far harder than commentary implies — the 2015/2016 Ukraine attacks required years of access and produced hours, not days, of outage, and Western grids restore manually. Adversaries also value pre-positioned access as deterrent leverage and burn it by using it. The strongest upward argument is that Iran, unlike Russia and China, may soon have little left to lose.

discrete_risks.name: The Islamic Republic ceases to govern Iran
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The office of Supreme Leader (Velayat-e Faqih) is abolished, vacated without a successor for more than 90 days, or a government not derived from the clerical/IRGC establishment exercises effective control of Tehran; as assessed by consensus of major-power governments.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The February 2026 decapitation killed Khamenei and dozens of senior military figures; Mojtaba Khamenei's succession is contested, with visible institutional friction (the 30 June state-TV censorship of Speaker Ghalibaf), spreading labour and student strikes across Tehran, Gilan and Kurdistan, surging armed attacks on regime forces, a blockaded economy and a wrecked deterrent. Analysts nonetheless expect short-term elite cohesion under external attack, with fragmentation more likely once the immediate crisis abates — which argues for the risk peaking in 2027-2029 rather than now.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Personalist/ideological revolutionary regimes surviving a decapitation strike plus mass protest plus economic blockade: Iraq 1991 (survived), Libya 2011 (fell, with air campaign plus ground rebels), Syria 2011-2024 (fell after 13 years), Serbia 2000 (fell). Roughly 3-4 of 8-10 comparable cases fell within a decade, but almost none within 18 months absent an occupying ground force.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The IRGC controls the economy, the security services and the succession machinery, and external attack is historically the single best predictor of regime consolidation, not collapse. Every serious Iran-collapse forecast since 1979 — 1980, 1988, 1999, 2009, 2019, 2022, 2025 — has been wrong. There is also no organised opposition capable of taking power, which is the usual binding constraint.

discrete_risks.name: A jihadist insurgent group controls a Sahelian national capital for >=7 days
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: JNIM, ISSP/ISWAP or a successor jihadist organisation exercises effective control of Bamako, Ouagadougou or Niamey (including the presidential palace and central districts) for at least seven consecutive days, per ACLED coding or UN/Security Council reporting.
discrete_risks.reasoning: JNIM's fuel blockade of Bamako has run since September 2025, strangling the Abidjan-Bamako corridor (~1.47 Mt of goods in 2025) and the Sikasso approaches; the group took Loulouni, staged seven simultaneous attacks in Kayes on the Senegal/Mauritania border, and has shifted from rural insurgency to capital strangulation. Mali's junta has lost Wagner/Africa Corps effectiveness and popular legitimacy. But strangulation is not seizure: JNIM's model is to make governments ungovernable and extract, not to hold cities that invite airpower.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Jihadist capture of a national capital: Kabul 1996 and 2021, Mogadishu 2006 (ICU). Three in ~30 years across all majority-Muslim insurgencies, all following the collapse of an externally-funded army. Mali 2012 came within ~600 km before French intervention. Unconditional rate ~1%/yr per at-risk capital; I use ~4%/yr for Bamako specifically.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Bamako has ~3 million people and the AES states plus Russia would face an existential incentive to intervene, as France did in 2013. JNIM has also repeatedly declined to take and hold urban centres where doing so would forfeit its negotiating position and expose it to airstrikes. Conversely, the Afghanistan 2021 lesson is that these transitions happen suddenly and forecasters were systematically too slow.

discrete_risks.name: US initiates withdrawal from NATO, or any member formally invokes Article 13
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The US President formally notifies the depositary of intent to withdraw under Article 13 of the North Atlantic Treaty, or any other member state does so.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The revealed 2026 strategy is not exit but renegotiation: the US signed the Ankara Declaration on 8 July 2026 reaffirming 5%/3.5% targets and announcing >$50bn in procurement, then began a posture review on 28 July aimed at making Europe carry conventional defence ('NATO 3.0'). Cuts are real (fighters 150->100, ISR 26->15, ~5,000 troops from Germany) but this is burden-shifting inside the alliance, which is cheaper and more useful to Washington than exit. The FY2024 NDAA also requires Senate consent or an act of Congress for withdrawal, and even Republican legislators publicly rebuked the drawdown.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: No state has ever invoked Article 13 in 77 years; France left the integrated command in 1966 without leaving the treaty, and Greece did similarly in 1974-80. Zero events in 77 years across ~30 members.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: De facto abandonment does not require de jure withdrawal, so this question may be measuring the wrong thing: an alliance whose guarantor has removed its forces and publicly conditioned its guarantee on spending is already hollowed out at Article 13 = 0%. If the model cares about Article 5 credibility rather than treaty membership, this risk is badly specified and the continuous US-posture variables matter far more.

discrete_risks.name: UN Security Council permanent membership formally expanded
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: An amendment to the UN Charter expanding the number of permanent Security Council members enters into force following ratification by two-thirds of member states including all five current permanent members.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Requires unanimous P5 ratification, and China blocks India/Japan, Russia blocks any Western-aligned addition, and the Africa/Ezulwini and G4/Uniting-for-Consensus blocs cancel each other. The 2026 environment — Council paralysis over Ukraine, Iran, Gaza and now the Venezuela intervention — increases the rhetorical demand for reform while decreasing the great-power comity needed to deliver it. India's BRICS presidency and the New Delhi summit will amplify the demand without changing the veto arithmetic.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: The Charter has been amended for Council composition exactly once, in 1965 (non-permanent seats 6->10), in 81 years. Permanent membership has never changed except by state succession (USSR->Russia, ROC->PRC). One near-miss event in 81 years.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: A settlement of the Ukraine war plus a US administration that treats institutions transactionally could conceivably produce a grand bargain (e.g. India and an African seat without veto) faster than the 60-year record suggests. Also, a partial reform — new permanent seats without veto — might be counted 'yes' by some resolvers, which would raise these numbers materially.

continuous_variables.name: World military expenditure as share of global GDP
continuous_variables.notes: SIPRI-verified 2025 value: 2.5%, highest since 2009, on $2,887bn total (+2.9% real, 11th straight rise). Drift reflects NATO's 3.5% core / 5% total by 2035 pledge (Ankara, July 2026), Europe +14% in 2025, Asia-Oceania +8.1%, offset by a declining US share. Roughly 5.5 years to end-2031: 2.5 + 0.075*5.5 = 2.91, sd = 0.10*sqrt(5.5) = 0.235.

continuous_variables.name: Global state-based armed conflict battle deaths per year
continuous_variables.notes: ACLED counted ~185,000 violent events in 2025 with state forces in 74% of them; Ukraine and Sudan dominate the fatality total. Drift is mildly negative on the assumption of an eventual Ukraine ceasefire (~42% by 2027, 78% by 2031), but the distribution is right-skewed: treat as lognormal, since a Taiwan or Korea contingency is a multi-hundred-thousand-death tail that the normal-drift parameters cannot represent.

continuous_variables.name: Brent crude oil price
continuous_variables.notes: Verified July 2026 path: eased to ~$70 in late June, spiked 9.5% to >$83 on the 14 July US Hormuz blockade announcement, closed at $85.87 then fell 11.3%. Treat as lognormal and mean-reverting to a $65-75 marginal-cost anchor, with a fat right tail conditional on Hormuz closure (geopolitics_hormuz_major_closure at 58% by 2027) and Bab el-Mandeb disruption. During the March 2026 closure Brent broke $100 and credible analysts modelled $150-200.

continuous_variables.name: US military expenditure as share of US GDP
continuous_variables.notes: SIPRI reported US spending declined in real terms in 2025 even as global spending rose - a genuinely important and underweighted fact. Drift is near-flat: Golden Dome ($185bn official, up to $1.2T over 20 years on independent estimates) and shipbuilding push up, while the Europe drawdown and fiscal pressure push down. Not independently verified against OMB; SIPRI-basis figure inferred.

continuous_variables.name: European NATO members' aggregate defence spending as share of GDP
continuous_variables.notes: European spending rose 14% in 2025 to $864bn (SIPRI); European allies plus Canada added $139bn in core defence requirements. The Ankara pledge is 3.5% core by 2035, implying ~0.09-0.13pp/yr from ~2.6%. Downside risk: fiscal limits and a Ukraine settlement removing urgency. Upside: the 28 July 2026 US posture review forcing Europe to fund enablers (ISR, tankers, deep fires) it currently rents from Washington.

continuous_variables.name: PLA aircraft sorties entering Taiwan's ADIZ per year
continuous_variables.notes: Verified record: 3,615 sorties in 2024 (Taiwan MND via Janes), vs 1,669 in 2023, 1,597 in 2022, 972 in 2021. 2025-2026 totals not verified this session; current_value assumes a plateau near the 2024 record. This is the cleanest continuous proxy for cross-Strait coercion intensity; step-changes cluster around Taiwanese elections (Jan 2028), high-profile US/Japanese visits, and Chinese domestic political events.

continuous_variables.name: US dollar share of allocated global FX reserves
continuous_variables.notes: NOT verified against IMF COFER this session; ~58% comes from 2026 press coverage of the BRICS agenda (down from a 2000 peak of ~71-88% depending on measure). Drift reflects a slow, real, decades-long diversification into gold and non-traditional currencies, accelerated by 2022 reserve immobilisation and 2026 US unilateralism, but NOT a BRICS currency: India has explicitly shelved that and says it has no policy to replace the dollar. Watch BRICS Pay and the gold-linked 'Unit' at the New Delhi summit as the real signal.

continuous_variables.name: Weekly container-ship transits of the Suez Canal
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: ~26/week in mid-January 2026 vs ~80/week pre-crisis; recovery has been slow and uneven, and most carriers still default to the Cape. Late July 2026 saw fresh deterioration as the Houthis declared a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb and two Saudi crude tankers reversed course. Maersk's 2026 guidance spans a $1.5bn loss to a $1.0bn profit purely on this uncertainty. Censored above at ~90 (physical/commercial ceiling).

continuous_variables.name: Combined US + Russia deployed strategic nuclear warheads
continuous_variables.notes: New START's 1,550-each ceiling lapsed 4-5 February 2026 with no successor and no talks. Both sides retain substantial upload capacity (US Minuteman III and Trident D5 downloaded warheads; Russian Sarmat/Yars MIRV capacity), so uploading is fast and cheap if either chooses. Drift assumes gradual, partly-signalled uploading driven by Golden Dome and Chinese expansion; a new agreement (30% by 2031) would truncate the upper tail. Note that after February 2026 there is no inspection regime, so this variable is now estimated, not measured - a genuine epistemic degradation.

continuous_variables.name: Net monthly Russian territorial gain in Ukraine
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: 622.6 km2 in Jan-Jun 2026 (~104/month) vs 2,189.9 km2 in Jan-Jun 2025 - a 72% collapse in the rate of advance, with Kostiantynivka gains limited to small-group infiltration that is not consolidating. Strongly bimodal and censored: conditional on a durable ceasefire the value pins near zero, and conditional on no ceasefire it likely stays in the 50-200 range. Do not model as a smooth Gaussian; use a regime-switching process gated on geopolitics_ukraine_durable_ceasefire.

continuous_variables.name: Number of active state-based armed conflicts (>=25 battle deaths/year)
continuous_variables.notes: UCDP-definition count; the 2024 figure of ~61 was a post-1946 record. NOT verified for 2025-2026 this session - inferred from ACLED's 'high levels of conflict became the new normal' framing and the resurgence of jihadist insurgencies noted in the Conflict Index 2026. Slight negative drift assumes Ukraine and possibly Lebanon/Gaza de-escalate; Sahel diffusion and Iran-linked proxy activation push the other way.

continuous_variables.name: Crude and condensate transiting the Strait of Hormuz
continuous_variables.notes: Pre-crisis baseline ~20 mb/d (roughly a fifth of global consumption). Current value is a rough inference, not a verified measurement: Iran has 'effectively shut' the strait per late-July reporting, the US has blockaded Iranian ports since 14 July with a 20% cargo fee, 24 tankers are queued at Kharg, and mine risk plus insurance withdrawal suppress transits well below any declared restriction. Censored above at ~21 (pipeline bypass capacity via East-West and ADCOP is only ~6.5 mb/d, so closure cannot be fully offset).

feedback_loops.name: Security-dilemma rearmament spiral
feedback_loops.mechanism: European rearmament (+14% in 2025, 3.5% GDP core pledge by 2035) and Golden Dome are read in Moscow and Beijing as offensive; they respond with missile and warhead expansion, which validates the original Western threat assessment and funds the next tranche. New START's expiry removed the transparency mechanism that previously damped the misperception term, so each side now sizes forces against worst-case estimates rather than inspected counts.

feedback_loops.name: Guarantor-withdrawal to proliferation cascade
feedback_loops.mechanism: US burden-shifting (Europe posture review, ~5,000 troops out of Germany, fighters 150->100) plus the demonstration that a non-nuclear state's leadership can be decapitated from the air (Iran, Feb 2026) raises the perceived value of an independent deterrent. ROK support runs 75-80%, Poland's president endorsed one in Feb 2026, Japan's taboo is eroding. Any one acquisition would sharply raise the incentive for the others and for their adversaries, while further devaluing the US guarantee that restrained them.

feedback_loops.name: Chokepoint shock to coalition fracture
feedback_loops.mechanism: Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb disruption raises oil prices, which mechanically raises Russian and Iranian export revenue and squeezes European and Asian importers. The July 2026 EU sanctions fight is the clean example: the Hormuz-driven price spike would have pushed the dynamic price cap from $44.10 to ~$58, handing Moscow a windfall, and the EU had to freeze the formula and buy off Greek shipping interests to prevent it. High prices thus weaken the sanctions coalitions that constrain the actors causing the disruption.

feedback_loops.name: Attrition-fiscal exhaustion
feedback_loops.mechanism: Russian monthly casualties (>30k) now exceed recruitment (~27k), the rate of territorial gain fell 72% year-on-year, the 2026 budget deficit allowance was exhausted by April and gold reserves are being drawn down at record pace. Sustained war mechanically degrades the capacity to sustain war, pushing both sides toward the settlement space and simultaneously reducing the residual Russian force available for NATO adventurism.

feedback_loops.name: Commercial hostage-taking restraint
feedback_loops.mechanism: Deep economic entanglement makes coercion self-harming and buys de-escalation. The 15 May 2026 Trump-Xi Beijing summit produced $17bn/yr agricultural purchases, 200 Boeing aircraft, restored beef and poultry access and standing Boards of Trade and Investment, and both sides want the November 2026 tariff truce extended - which materially lowered near-term Taiwan risk. The same logic constrains Iran (its own exports transit Hormuz) and China-Japan (Beijing chose seafood bans over ships).

feedback_loops.name: Sanctions-evasion capability accumulation
feedback_loops.mechanism: Each sanctions escalation (21 EU packages, 218 designations in July 2026 alone, 41 more shadow-fleet vessels, the first LNG measures) prompts investment in evasion infrastructure - shadow fleets, bunkering networks, crewing agencies, BRICS Pay rails, CBDC interoperability, gold settlement. That infrastructure is durable and reusable, so the marginal deterrent value of the next sanctions package falls, requiring broader and more intrusive measures that push more states toward the alternative rails.

feedback_loops.name: Successful-coercion imitation
feedback_loops.mechanism: Low-cost US successes (Maduro seized in Caracas with zero US casualties, Jan 2026; Khamenei killed in a 900-strike opening salvo, Feb 2026) update every actor's estimate of what unilateral force can achieve and what the international system will tolerate. This raises US willingness to repeat, raises other revisionists' expectation of impunity for their own faits accomplis, and raises target states' incentive to pre-position deterrents (dispersal, nuclear latency, hostage-taking of commercial traffic).

feedback_loops.name: Gray-zone ratchet under the Article 5 threshold
feedback_loops.mechanism: Because Russia's hybrid operations (Sandworm wipers on ~30 Polish energy sites, shadow-ship-launched drones closing European airports, cable cuts, sabotage) reliably produce Article 4 consultations rather than Article 5, the expected cost stays low and the tempo rises. Each unanswered increment establishes the next one as normal, which both erodes deterrence and steadily raises the probability that some future increment overshoots into an unintended mass-casualty event.

feedback_loops.name: External-threat elite consolidation, then post-crisis fragmentation
feedback_loops.mechanism: In regimes under attack, external pressure suppresses factional conflict in the short run because visible fragmentation invites further escalation - the documented dynamic in post-Khamenei Iran through mid-2026. This is balancing on a 1-2 year horizon but flips sign afterward: once the acute threat abates, the suppressed rivalries surface with accumulated grievances, which is why Iranian instability risk likely peaks in 2027-2029 rather than in 2026.

structural_uncertainties: Leadership mortality and succession are the largest unmodelled discontinuity. Putin (73), Trump (80), Khamenei's untested successor Mojtaba, Kim Jong Un's health, and Xi's post-purge PLA all sit on single points of failure. A single actuarial event could invert the sign of several of these forecasts within weeks, and no reference class gives useful conditional probabilities for what follows. The 2026 Iranian case shows that even an externally-imposed succession produces outcomes (short-run consolidation) opposite to the intuitive prediction.

The February 2026 Iran campaign may have established a new operative norm - that decapitating a nuclear-threshold state's leadership from the air is a usable policy option - rather than being a one-off. If so, the entire deterrence architecture this model assumes is wrong: proliferation demand jumps discontinuously, launch-on-warning postures tighten, and 'crisis stability' calculations built on 1960s-1980s logic no longer describe how leaders reason about survivability.

AI's effect on military balance, escalation speed and intelligence is genuinely indeterminate and could dominate everything else by 2031. Autonomous drone swarms may make amphibious invasion impossible (favouring Taiwan) or make blockade cheap and deniable (favouring Beijing); AI-enabled ISR may make second-strike submarines findable, which would be the single most destabilising technical development since MIRVs. Nothing in my continuous variables captures this.

Measurement itself is degrading. New START's expiry ended strategic warhead verification; the IAEA has lost effective access to Iran; Russian and Ukrainian casualty figures span factors of two to three across credible sources; and Chinese defence spending is systematically understated by the official 1.91tn yuan figure. Several of my indicators are now estimates of estimates, and confident quantitative modelling on top of them may create false precision precisely where the underlying uncertainty is widening.

The binary framing of 'war' may be obsolete. The most consequential 2026 events - a fee-and-blockade regime on a strait, wiper malware in a power grid, a fuel blockade of a capital by a non-state group, shadow-ship drones closing airports - do not resolve cleanly as war or peace. A model built on discrete conflict-onset events will systematically miss the actual mechanism by which the order is changing, which is continuous coercion below every declared threshold.

Domestic political discontinuity in the United States is a first-order geopolitical variable that this domain model treats as exogenous. The November 2026 midterms, the 2028 election, and the constitutional questions raised by the Venezuela and Iran operations could reverse the burden-shifting doctrine, the Golden Dome programme, the Ukraine posture and the Gulf commitment simultaneously - or entrench them. Correlation across all my risks through this single channel is high and unmodelled.

Economic regime change could dominate the security model. A Chinese property/demographic hard landing, an AI-driven productivity boom, an energy transition that halves the strategic value of Hormuz, or a US fiscal crisis forcing real defence cuts would each rewrite the drift terms on nearly every continuous variable here. The 2.5%-of-GDP military burden assumes growth continues to fund it.

I may be systematically anchored on the last six months. H1 2026 was extraordinarily eventful, which biases toward extrapolating high-tempo conflict. The honest base-rate view is that most years contain no great-power war, most crises de-escalate, and the modal 2027-2031 looks more like grinding normality than like H1 2026 repeated ten times. If I am miscalibrated, the most likely direction is that my 2031 and 2036 cumulative numbers are collectively too high.

research.state_of_play:
As of late July 2026 the dominant near-term fact in this domain is a rapidly intensifying, possibly record-strength El Niño. I verified that NOAA CPC put El Niño emergence at 82% for May-Jul 2026 and 96% for Dec 2026-Feb 2027, that NOAA declared a "Super El Niño" underway on 11 June 2026 with a 63% chance of a "very strong" event, and that GFDL's July SPEAR run has all 30 ensemble members peaking at strengths competitive with the strongest events of the past century, peaking late 2026. ECMWF's median Niño3.4 peak is around +3.0C for December with high-end members near +4C. I treat the more extreme multi-model medians circulating (e.g. +3.59C) with skepticism: no event in 150 years of record has meaningfully exceeded +2.75C, and dynamical models have historically overshot super-event forecasts (2014 being the canonical bust). The physically defensible read is a very strong event that is more likely than not to rival 1997-98 and 2015-16, with a real chance of setting a record and a meaningful chance of underperforming the hype.

Global temperature has been in a relative lull. Verified: H1 2026 was the third-warmest start on record in all six major datasets, behind 2024 and 2025, at roughly 1.4C above pre-industrial. January was fifth-warmest (12.95C, +0.51C vs 1991-2020), April joint third (14.89C, +1.43C above pre-industrial), while May and June were both second-warmest globally as El Niño took hold. June was the hottest June on record for western Europe. Carbon Brief's record-year probability for 2026 rose from 19% in April to 35% in July; Polymarket prices 2026 at ~31% for warmest and ~60% for second-warmest, with ~85% odds on at least one record month. The critical implication is that 2027, not 2026, is the likely record year — the 2015/2016 analogue puts peak global response roughly a year after the Niño3.4 peak.

Ocean state is extreme. Global SST anomaly hit +0.5C on 30 June 2026, the highest ever for that date; H1 2026 was the second-warmest ocean half-year at ~20.94C. Ocean heat content set a record for the ninth consecutive year in 2025 (+23±8 ZJ, 0-2000m). In 2025, 89% of the global ocean saw at least one marine heatwave and 55% saw strong-or-worse. The fourth global coral bleaching event, declared April 2024, remains active; 84.4% of global reef area saw bleaching-level stress between Jan 2023 and Sep 2025. Every strong El Niño since 1998 has coincided with a global bleaching event, so reef outcomes in 2026-27 are likely to be historically bad.

Cryosphere: Arctic winter maximum on 15 March 2026 was 14.29 million km², statistically tied with 2025 for the lowest on record and 1.36 million km² below the 1981-2010 average. Antarctic sea ice, notably, rebounded — the 26 February 2026 minimum of 2.58 million km² ranked only 16th lowest, ending four years of record/near-record lows, driven by Weddell Sea wind anomalies rather than any thermodynamic reprieve. Greenland lost 139 Gt in the 2024-25 hydrological year. Sea level rise is running ~4.5-5.9 mm/yr with acceleration of ~0.83 mm/yr/decade.

Emissions have plateaued but not peaked. GCP put 2025 fossil CO2 at a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.1%); IEA put energy CO2 at 38.4 Gt (+0.4%) and forecasts power-sector emissions plateauing 2026-2030. China's emissions fell 0.3% in 2025 and have been flat-or-falling for 21 months. The remaining 1.5C budget is ~170 GtCO2, about four years. Mauna Loa CO2 was 431.44 ppm in June 2026; the 2026 annual mean is forecast at 429.4±0.6 ppm (+2.37 ppm). Methane reached ~1938 ppb at Mauna Loa in March 2026 and continues accelerating.

Policy has bifurcated. The US Paris withdrawal took effect January 2026 and EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding on 12 February 2026 (effective 20 April), now in D.C. Circuit litigation. Countervailing: the ICJ's July 2025 advisory opinion was operationalized by UNGA resolution A/80/L.65 on 20 May 2026, and domestic courts in Costa Rica, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Canada have already cited it. UNEP's 2025 Emissions Gap Report puts NDC-implied warming at 2.3-2.5C. COP31 convenes in Antalya 9-20 November 2026 under a Turkey/Australia split arrangement.

Not verified this session and drawn from pre-2026 knowledge: exact ERA5 2025 annual anomaly, IPCC AR7 timeline specifics, COP32 host, current RAPID AMOC transport values, and September 2026 Arctic minimum (not yet occurred).
