scheduled_events.name: EU AI Act: Commission GPAI enforcement powers and penalties activate (up to €15M / 3% turnover); Art.50 synthetic-media transparency applies
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First moment the EU can actually fine frontier model providers. Sets precedent for whether the AI Act has teeth or becomes a paper regime.

scheduled_events.name: Nvidia Q2 FY2027 earnings (guided ~$91B revenue)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The single highest-information event for the AI capex cycle. A miss or soft guide during an ongoing Nasdaq correction would be the clearest bubble-deflation trigger.

scheduled_events.name: US interagency assessment of nucleic acid synthesis screening framework due
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Determines whether DNA synthesis screening becomes mandatory in the US as AI protein-design tools erode existing sequence-based screens.

scheduled_events.name: US midterm elections
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Datacenter electricity bills and AI job anxiety are live campaign issues; outcome shapes whether federal preemption of state AI law is achievable in the 120th Congress.

scheduled_events.name: Hyperscaler Q4-2026 earnings with initial 2027 capex guidance
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The first collective statement on whether the ~$700B/yr buildout continues, plateaus, or is cut. Highest-leverage scheduled data point for the whole domain.

scheduled_events.name: Oracle–OpenAI ~$300B / 4.5GW compute contract begins
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Converts a paper commitment into cash obligations for a company with ~$25B ARR; a stress test of the circular-financing structure underpinning AI capex.

scheduled_events.name: California TFAIA first annual frontier-model transparency reports
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First mandatory public disclosure regime for US frontier labs; establishes whether state-level transparency survives federal preemption pressure.

scheduled_events.name: EU AI Act: Annex III high-risk obligations apply (deferred from 2026-08 by Digital Omnibus)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The main compliance burden for AI deployers in hiring, credit, education, and law enforcement. Slippage again would signal Europe has effectively deregulated.

scheduled_events.name: EU AI Act: Annex I product-embedded high-risk obligations apply
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Extends the regime to medical devices, machinery, and vehicles — the point at which AI regulation intersects physical product liability.

scheduled_events.name: IBM Starling: targeted first large-scale fault-tolerant quantum system (200 logical qubits, 100M gates)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: If met, marks the start of a credible countdown to cryptographically relevant quantum computing; if missed by years, deflates Q-day urgency.

scheduled_events.name: US CNSA 2.0 / NIST post-quantum migration milestones for federal and national security systems
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Forces the practical cost of 'harvest now, decrypt later' onto real budgets regardless of whether quantum hardware arrives.

scheduled_events.name: China domestic DUV lithography scale-up to ~20 units/year
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The measurable test of whether Chinese lithography self-sufficiency is real. Determines the residual leverage of US export controls after 2028.

discrete_risks.name: A top-4 US hyperscaler guides annual capex down year-over-year
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, or Meta states in an official earnings release or call that its expected full-fiscal-year capital expenditures will be LOWER than the prior fiscal year's actual capex.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2026 guidance is ~$600-725B, roughly double 2025, at 45-57% of revenue. All four claim supply-constraint, not demand-constraint, and have multi-year land/power/lease commitments that make a fast reversal costly. But depreciation from the 2025-26 vintage hits P&L hard in 2027-28, and the Nasdaq 100 is already in correction on exactly this concern. A digestion year within five is close to the historical norm for any capital cycle of this intensity.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: large-cap capital cycles. Telecom capex fell YoY in 2001-02 after the fiber boom; semiconductor capex fell YoY in 1998, 2001, 2009, 2019, 2023. Hyperscaler capex has fallen YoY only once (Meta 2023) in the last decade — roughly 1 event per 40 company-years recently, but ~1 in 6 years across broader capital-intensive tech.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Compute demand may genuinely be inference-driven and structurally growing; if token volumes keep compounding and agentic deployment sticks, capex could rise every single year through 2031 and this resolves NO even in 2036. Also, companies can reclassify spending into leases and off-balance-sheet SPVs to avoid a formal guide-down, making the criterion under-inclusive.

discrete_risks.name: Nvidia suffers a ≥50% peak-to-trough drawdown
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Nvidia's split-adjusted closing share price falls at least 50% below its all-time closing high, at any point in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Nvidia is already in a semiconductor selloff that erased >$1.3T of sector value in June 2026, with the Nasdaq 100 in correction as of July 28. Concentration risk is extreme: a handful of customers fund most of data center revenue, several with circular financing. A 50% drawdown does not require a thesis break, only a growth-rate disappointment against ~90% YoY comps.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Nvidia specifically has had ≥50% drawdowns in 2002, 2008, 2018, and 2022 — 4 episodes in ~24 years, ~17%/yr unconditional. High-multiple semis in general: ≥50% drawdowns roughly every 5-7 years.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Nvidia at ~$300B+ annualized data center revenue with real earnings is a fundamentally different animal than in 2018 or 2022; earnings growth can absorb multiple compression without a 50% price decline. If CoWoS-constrained supply keeps shipping out, the drawdown may cap at 30-40%.

discrete_risks.name: Frontier agent reaches a 1-work-month 50%-reliability task horizon
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: METR (or a successor methodology it endorses) publishes a 50%-reliability time horizon of ≥167 hours of human-expert task time for a publicly deployed or externally evaluated frontier model.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Current frontier is plausibly 2-15 hours (sources conflict badly). Reaching 167h needs roughly 4-6 doublings. At the historical 7-month doubling that is 2.3-3.5 years; at the claimed recent 4-month doubling it is 1.3-2 years. Against that: METR's own data shows a sharp reliability cliff (near-100% on <4-minute tasks, <10% on >4-hour tasks), long-horizon tasks are messier and less verifiable than the benchmark suite, and measurement gets harder as tasks lengthen — METR may simply stop being able to run the eval.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: exponential capability trends in computing that persisted 6+ years. Moore's Law, transistor counts, and ImageNet error all held for a decade+; but Bloom filters of AI-specific trends (e.g. chess Elo, ALE scores) typically bent or saturated within 5-8 years. Base rate for a 6-year exponential continuing another 3 years: ~50-60%.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The time-horizon metric may be measuring benchmark-suite fit rather than general autonomy; if the underlying task distribution isn't representative, 167h could be hit on paper in 2028 while real-world month-long autonomous work remains impossible. Conversely, if AI-automated AI research kicks in, this could resolve YES by 2028 and my 2027 number is far too low.

discrete_risks.name: A Fortune 500 firm announces ≥10,000 job cuts explicitly attributed primarily to AI
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A Fortune 500 (US) or Fortune Global 500 company announces a workforce reduction of ≥10,000 positions in a single announcement, and its official communications name AI/automation as the primary stated cause (not merely one factor among several).
discrete_risks.reasoning: Large layoffs at this scale happen regularly; the binding constraint is the ATTRIBUTION, which carries legal, PR, and morale costs — firms prefer 'restructuring' or 'efficiency'. But the norm is shifting: AI-attributed cuts already ran ~49,000 announced in H1 2026 per TrueUp/Challenger-style trackers, and being seen as AI-forward now helps the stock. Employment-weighted AI adoption at ~32% and rising makes the claim credible.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: single-announcement layoffs ≥10,000 at F500 firms occur roughly 5-15 times per year globally (IBM 1993, HP 2012/2015, IBM 2023, Amazon 2022-23, Intel 2024-25). The conditional question is attribution, which has gone from ~0% of such announcements pre-2023 to a nonzero minority in 2025-26.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Firms have strong incentive to blame macro conditions instead — Bloomberg-covered research (June 2026) finds weak hiring, not AI, dominates young-worker outcomes, and legal exposure (WARN, age/disparate-impact claims) discourages naming AI. This could stay perpetually just below the explicit-attribution bar.

discrete_risks.name: US unemployment rate ≥6.0% for three consecutive months
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: BLS headline U-3 seasonally adjusted unemployment rate is at or above 6.0% in three consecutive monthly releases.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Included as the cross-domain node where AI displacement, AI-capex-driven growth, and monetary conditions interact. Currently unemployment is in the mid-4s with no detectable aggregate AI effect (Dallas Fed, Anthropic Economic Index, St. Louis Fed all agree). But the AI capex cycle is now a material share of US GDP growth; a capex bust would itself be recessionary independent of displacement.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Since 1948, U-3 has been ≥6.0% in ~33% of months. US recessions occur roughly once per 6-8 years (~14%/yr hazard); most but not all push unemployment above 6%. From a mid-4s starting point, a 1.4-year horizon gives ~15-22%.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: AI could be net job-creating in aggregate through the window while displacing specific cohorts, and the labor market has repeatedly absorbed technology shocks without aggregate unemployment. Also, this is dominated by monetary policy and fiscal conditions, not AI — attributing it to this domain is a modeling convenience, not a causal claim.

discrete_risks.name: A Chinese-developed model holds #1 on a major independent aggregate leaderboard for ≥1 month
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A model developed by a China-headquartered organization holds the top overall rank on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index or LMArena's overall text leaderboard continuously for at least 30 days.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Chinese open-weight models now consume ~61% of OpenRouter tokens and sit within single-digit points on SWE-bench-style suites, but the very top of the reasoning distribution is still Western (Claude Opus 5 at 61 on the AA index, July 24 2026). Chinese labs are compute-constrained by export controls and by Beijing's own refusal to buy licensed H200s. Domestic DUV production and Ascend scale-up narrow this over 3-5 years.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Chinese entrants reaching #1 in a Western-measured technology leaderboard. Precedents exist (TOP500 supercomputing 2010-2017, EV battery energy density, 5G patents) — typically 5-10 years after entering the top tier. Chinese frontier LLMs entered the top tier in 2024-25.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Leaderboards are gameable and Chinese labs optimize hard for them; a nominal #1 could arrive much sooner than genuine parity, making my 2027 number too low. Conversely, if compute controls bite harder than expected and Beijing keeps restricting Nvidia purchases without adequate domestic substitution, Chinese labs could plateau and this never resolves.

discrete_risks.name: China demonstrates a domestically built EUV lithography tool patterning wafers in a production fab
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Credible public confirmation (company announcement, government statement, or two independent major-outlet reports) that a China-built EUV scanner is exposing wafers in a commercial production fab, not merely a lab or prototype.
discrete_risks.reasoning: China only just reached mass production of immersion DUV (July 2026: 5 units this year, ~20 in 2027), which ASML shipped in 2004. EUV is a far larger jump — tin-droplet LPP source power, multilayer Mo/Si mirror figuring to picometer tolerance, and a supply chain (Zeiss, Trumpf, Cymer) with no domestic analogue. Chinese EUV remains at prototype stage. State funding is effectively unlimited and the timeline pressure is existential, which is why I do not put this below 40% by 2031.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: national programs replicating a monopoly capital-equipment technology under sanction. ASML took ~17 years from EUV program start to HVM. Soviet/Chinese jet engine and lithography replication efforts historically ran 10-20 years behind, often with 'demonstration' well before volume. China's EUV program is ~6-8 years old.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Chinese officials and state media have repeatedly announced lithography 'breakthroughs' that did not translate to fab use; my resolution criterion may be met by a heavily publicized, economically irrelevant single tool. Alternatively, China may route around EUV entirely via DUV multipatterning plus advanced packaging and chiplets, making the milestone never worth pursuing at production scale.

discrete_risks.name: US licenses its current-flagship datacenter GPU for general commercial sale to China
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: BIS policy permits general (not narrowly case-by-case) export to Chinese commercial customers of Nvidia's then-current top-of-line datacenter accelerator, within one product generation of the US-available flagship.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Policy already moved this direction: H200 approved for China in Dec 2025 with a 25% surcharge, and Nvidia is actively lobbying using the Huawei-substitution argument. But H200 is two generations behind the flagship, and Beijing has refused to buy, which paradoxically reduces US incentive to relax further. Congressional China hawks and the GAIN-AI-style legislative push cut the other way.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US export control regimes on a strategic technology being substantially liberalized within a decade. COCOM computing controls liberalized repeatedly in the 1990s; encryption export controls relaxed in 1999-2000 after ~7 years; satellite controls tightened rather than relaxed. Roughly 1 in 3 regimes liberalize within a decade once domestic substitution appears.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Controls could tighten instead — a Chinese military AI incident or a Taiwan crisis would ratchet restrictions to near-total. Also, the whole question may go moot if Chinese domestic accelerators reach good-enough parity and Beijing bans Nvidia purchases outright, in which case 'licensed for sale' becomes meaningless.

discrete_risks.name: AI-orchestrated cyberattack causes ≥$1B damage or a national-scale critical-infrastructure disruption
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A government agency, CERT, or the victim organization publicly confirms an attack in which AI agents autonomously executed the majority of intrusion steps, AND documented direct losses exceed $1B (2026 USD) or the attack disrupted power, water, telecom, or payments service for >1 million people for >6 hours.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The precursor already happened: Anthropic's GTG-1002 disclosure (Nov 2025) showed a Chinese state-linked actor running ~30 target intrusions with Claude executing 80-90% of steps autonomously. OpenAI has classified GPT-5.4 as 'High' cyber capability under its Preparedness Framework. What is missing is the damage scale and the attribution clarity. Attribution of AI autonomy is the hard part — most incident reports will not be able to establish it.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: cyberattacks with ≥$1B documented damage. NotPetya (2017, ~$10B), WannaCry (2017, ~$4-8B), Change Healthcare (2024, ~$2.5B+), MOVEit (2023, ~$12B est.). Roughly 1 per 1-2 years globally. The AI-attribution conditional is the binding constraint, currently maybe 10-25% of such events and rising.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: AI is symmetrically empowering defenders — automated patching, anomaly detection, and code auditing may improve faster than offense because defenders have vastly more compute and data. Also, damage estimates and 'majority autonomous' claims are both soft; this could stay perpetually unresolvable rather than clearly NO.

discrete_risks.name: AI-assisted biological attack causing ≥10 deaths, officially confirmed
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A national government, WHO, or equivalent official body confirms a deliberate biological release causing ≥10 human deaths, and officially states that AI tools materially assisted the design, synthesis planning, or acquisition of the agent.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is where narrative pull is strongest and calibration matters most. Bioterrorism with ≥10 deaths is astonishingly rare regardless of information availability, because the binding constraints are tacit wet-lab skill, agent stability, aerosolization, and the near-total absence of actors who both want mass casualties and can execute. AI uplift estimates are modest on knowledge (RAND 2024: 1.0-1.2x) but concerning on screening evasion (2-3x, potentially 7-10x by 2028). Screening improved sharply (~40-70% to ~97% post-patch) after generative protein design was shown to evade it.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: deliberate biological releases causing ≥10 deaths, worldwide, ever. Essentially: none in the modern era. The 2001 anthrax letters killed 5. Aum Shinrikyo's biological program killed 0 despite years of effort, a PhD team, and a $1B budget. Base rate is well under 1 event per 25 years globally.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The honest contrarian case is that I am too low: AI agents that can plan and execute multi-step lab protocols, combined with cloud labs and unscreened benchtop synthesizers, could collapse the tacit-knowledge barrier faster than screening norms adapt — and the Oct 13 2026 US interagency review may produce nothing binding. If the skill barrier is what has kept the base rate at zero, and AI removes it, historical frequency is worthless as a guide.

discrete_risks.name: US Congress enacts broad federal preemption of state AI laws
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A bill preempting state AI regulation across a broad category (beyond a single narrow domain like deepfakes) is signed into law by the President.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The administration wants it: EO 14365 (Dec 2025) created an AI Litigation Task Force and the March 20 2026 National Policy Framework explicitly recommends preemption. But Congress has already rejected it once decisively — the Senate stripped the 10-year moratorium from the OBBBA 99-1. Preemption requires 60 Senate votes and splits both parties (federalism conservatives + consumer-protection Democrats against). Post-midterm composition is the key variable.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: major federal preemption of an active state regulatory area. Examples: ERISA (1974), Airline Deregulation Act (1978), Telecom Act (1996), FDAAA. Federal privacy preemption has been attempted and failed for ~20 years straight — the closest analogue, and it suggests low odds.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The federal privacy analogue may mislead: AI has a genuine industry-wide constituency, a supportive executive, and a compliance-patchwork argument that resonates. Alternatively, preemption could arrive de facto via litigation and agency action without any statute, making this resolve NO while the substantive outcome is identical.

discrete_risks.name: Binding US-China agreement on frontier AI compute or model thresholds
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The US and China both sign a treaty, executive agreement, or equivalent binding instrument containing specific, verifiable commitments on frontier AI training compute limits, model capability thresholds, or mutual inspection.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The India AI Impact Summit (Feb 2026, 91 signatories) deliberately moved AWAY from safety and toward deployment/impact framing, and produced only voluntary instruments. US-China technology relations are in an active controls-and-retaliation cycle. Verification is technically hard — compute is fungible and inference clusters are indistinguishable from training clusters at a distance. The historical precondition for arms control (mutual demonstrated catastrophic capability, plus a scare) has not occurred.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: binding bilateral US-adversary technology arms control. SALT I took ~10 years from the enabling technology; the BWC took ~20; the NPT ~23. Cyber and space arms control have produced nothing binding in 30 years despite continuous negotiation. Roughly 1 success per 20-30 years, conditional on a salient shared threat.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: A sufficiently visible AI-caused catastrophe (a mass-casualty cyber or bio event with clear AI fingerprints) could compress the arms-control timeline dramatically — the Cuban Missile Crisis produced the hotline in under a year. My probabilities assume no such forcing event, which is itself an assumption.

discrete_risks.name: A top-5 Western frontier lab exits frontier training
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: One of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, or Meta Superintelligence Labs is acquired, dissolved, files for bankruptcy protection, or publicly announces it will stop pretraining frontier-scale models.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Frontier training now costs $200M-$500M per run rising toward $1-3B by late 2027, against real but insufficient revenue (OpenAI ~$25B ARR vs ~$14B losses and $80-100B/yr forward compute commitments). Meta and xAI are the most plausible exits: Meta can absorb the loss but has repeatedly restructured its AI org, and xAI has the thinnest revenue base. A capex-cycle downturn plus an AI-equity drawdown would make the marginal lab's next funding round very hard.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: top-5 players in a capital-intensive frontier technology exiting within a decade. Search engines (of the 1999 top 5, 3 exited by 2009); smartphone OS (Symbian, BlackBerry, Windows Phone all exited within 8 years); GPU vendors (3dfx, S3, Matrox exited within 5 years of the 1998 top 5). Historically ~40-60% of a top-5 cohort loses at least one member per decade.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: All five are backed by entities with effectively unlimited balance sheets (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Musk, sovereign funds). Strategic value alone justifies continued funding even at zero return, so 'exit' may simply never happen in the resolvable sense — the lab shrinks, pivots to inference and products, and quietly stops leading without ever announcing it.

discrete_risks.name: A US state enacts a statutory moratorium or hard cap on new large datacenter interconnections
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A US state enacts into law (governor's signature or veto override) a moratorium, ban, or binding numerical cap on new datacenter grid interconnections above a stated size threshold, applying statewide.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The political preconditions are already met: PJM capacity cleared at the $329.17/MW-day cap (11x the 2024-25 price), NRDC projects ~$70/month household bill increases by 2028, at least six states have introduced moratorium bills, seven are restricting tax incentives, and Oregon created a dedicated datacenter rate class. What has NOT happened is any state actually enacting a statewide hard moratorium — states are choosing rate-class reform and cost-allocation instead, which is the economically smarter tool. Local moratoria are common; statewide is the bar.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: state-level moratoria on a specific industrial land use following a rate/environmental backlash. New York's fracking moratorium (2010, enacted after 2 years of pressure), state crypto-mining moratoria (New York 2022, ~1 of 50 states within 3 years of the backlash peak), offshore drilling bans. Roughly 1 state in 50 acts within 2-4 years of peak salience.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: States compete aggressively for datacenter investment and jobs; the likelier equilibrium is cost-shifting (make datacenters pay their own capacity costs) rather than prohibition, which would leave this at NO indefinitely while still materially slowing the buildout. My criterion may therefore miss the real dynamic.

discrete_risks.name: A quantum computer publicly factors an RSA-2048 modulus
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A verifiable public demonstration in which a quantum computer factors a 2048-bit RSA modulus, with the factorization independently confirmed and the computation not reducible to classical pre-processing or special-structure moduli.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Physical requirements remain roughly 4-20 million physical qubits at current error rates, or ~thousands of high-quality logical qubits. Google's Willow demonstrated below-threshold surface-code memory at 105 physical qubits; IBM's roadmap targets 200 logical qubits and 100M gates by 2029 (Starling) — that is still 1-2 orders of magnitude short in logical qubit count and 3+ in gate depth. Algorithmic improvements (Gidney 2025) have cut requirements substantially and could cut them again, which is why 2036 is not 1%.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: quantum computing milestones hitting their published roadmap dates. IBM, Google, IonQ, and Rigetti roadmaps have slipped by 2-5 years each on nearly every multi-year target since 2018. Also: predicted 'X years to RSA' has been 10-20 years continuously since 1999 — a classic constant-horizon forecast.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Algorithmic resource estimates for Shor's have fallen ~20x in the last 5 years (better magic-state distillation, approximate modular arithmetic, yoked surface codes); another comparable improvement plus faster-than-roadmap logical qubit scaling could pull this into the early 2030s. A classified state capability would also not resolve this publicly.

discrete_risks.name: US driverless robotaxi services exceed 5 million paid rides per week
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Publicly reported paid rides in fully driverless (no human safety operator in vehicle) commercial services in the US total ≥5,000,000 in a single week, summed across all operators.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Waymo is at ~500k/week (July 2026) across 10+ cities, announced San Diego, Las Vegas, Tampa, Denver on July 8, and targets 1M/week by end-2026 — implying ~2x/year. Reaching 5M requires another ~2.3 doublings, i.e. late 2028-2029 at that pace. The constraints are vehicle manufacturing, depot buildout, and city-by-city regulatory approval rather than autonomy software, which is now demonstrably adequate. Tesla's robotaxi has not scaled meaningfully since Austin.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US rideshare adoption. Uber went from ~1M to ~50M US rides/week over roughly 2012-2018 (6 years), constrained by driver supply rather than capital. Waymo's constraint is capital and manufacturing, historically slower but more predictable. Total US rideshare is ~40-60M rides/week, so 5M is ~10% penetration.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: A single high-profile fatality involving a driverless vehicle could trigger multi-state suspensions and set the timeline back years — this happened to Uber ATG (2018) and Cruise (2023), both of which effectively ended those programs. Unit economics also remain unproven at scale; if per-ride costs don't fall below human drivers, growth stalls at premium-market saturation.

discrete_risks.name: A top mathematics journal publishes a paper whose central theorem was found primarily by AI
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A paper appears in Annals of Mathematics, JAMS, Inventiones, Acta Mathematica, or Duke Mathematical Journal in which the authors explicitly state that the principal new theorem was discovered or proved primarily by an AI system rather than by the human authors.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The substrate exists: ~100 Erdős problems moved to 'solved' with AI assistance since Oct 2025 per Tao's tracking, and OpenAI reported an internal model disproving a long-standing conjecture on the planar unit distance problem in May 2026. Several mathematicians predicted 2026 would be the first year AI-contributed results clear peer review in major journals. But top-5 journals are a much higher bar than 'a journal' — they publish deep structural results, and their referee cycles run 1-3 years. The Erdős problems being solved are mostly not top-5-journal material.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: computer-assisted proofs reaching flagship journals. Four Color Theorem (1977, but in Illinois J. Math); Kepler conjecture (Hales, Annals 2005 — ~7 years from proof to publication); Feit-Thompson formalization. Historically 5-15 years from first computational result to flagship acceptance, though referee culture is warming fast.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Attribution is the weak point: human authors have every professional incentive to describe AI as a tool rather than the discoverer, and journals have no disclosure requirement. The substantive event could occur repeatedly by 2028 while this criterion never resolves YES. Conversely, if a lab publishes directly with an AI credited, this could resolve much sooner than my 2027 number.

discrete_risks.name: A single training run of ≥1e28 FLOP is publicly reported
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Epoch AI, a lab's own technical report, or two independent credible technical analyses attribute ≥1e28 FLOP of training compute to a single model training run.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2026 frontier runs sit at 1e26-1e27 FLOP. At the historical 4-5x/year that reaches 1e28 in roughly 1.5-3 years — but three things push back: labs have stopped disclosing compute (making 'publicly reported' the binding constraint), training-run length cannot extend much further (Epoch), and power/packaging are now the binding physical constraints (CoWoS sold out, PJM capacity at cap). Also, post-training RL compute is increasingly separated from pretraining, muddying what counts as 'a single run'.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the 4.7x/yr frontier compute trend has held since 2020 (6 years) and the broader trend since 2010. Extrapolating a 6-year exponential 2 more years: ~70% historically. Extrapolating 5 more: ~50%. Discount ~25-30% for disclosure opacity.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Disclosure is the real risk to this resolving: OpenAI has not published compute figures since GPT-4, and Epoch's estimates are increasingly indirect. The physical event may well occur by 2028 while the reporting criterion fails. On the other side, if the paradigm shifts decisively to inference-time and RL compute, nobody may ever build a 1e28 single pretraining run because it isn't the efficient use of the cluster.

continuous_variables.name: Log10 of training compute for the largest publicly-known training run
continuous_variables.notes: Current value ~5e26 FLOP, consistent with Epoch's statement that 2026 frontier runs sit between 1e26 and 1e27 and that 1e26 was crossed in Nov 2025. Drift of 0.42 log10/yr equals ~2.6x/yr — deliberately BELOW the historical 4.7x/yr because power, CoWoS packaging, and maximum feasible run length are now binding, and because disclosure is degrading. p90 of 29.5 (~3e29) is near the plausible physical ceiling for a single 2031 run given multi-GW cluster limits.

continuous_variables.name: Global data center electricity consumption
continuous_variables.notes: Anchored on IEA's 415 TWh for 2024 plus verified +17% growth in 2025 (AI-specific DC load +50%), giving ~590 TWh for 2026. IEA base case is 945 TWh by 2030 and 1200 TWh by 2035, so my p50 of 1030 for 2031 is modestly above IEA base. Right tail reflects a scenario where the buildout continues unabated; left tail reflects a capex bust plus efficiency gains (better inference kernels, sparse models, custom ASICs).

continuous_variables.name: Combined annual capex, Microsoft + Alphabet + Amazon + Meta
continuous_variables.notes: 2026 guidance is ~$600-725B (verified), roughly double 2025. Very high vol relative to drift is intentional: this is the single most reflexive variable in the domain, and the Nasdaq 100 is already in correction over exactly this line item. The p10 of $470B is a genuine digestion/bust scenario (a ~33% cut from 2026), which I think is meaningfully more likely than a smooth-growth model implies.

continuous_variables.name: Nvidia annual data center revenue
continuous_variables.notes: Q1 FY2027 data center revenue of $75.2B with Q2 guided to ~$91B total implies a ~$330B annualized data center run-rate. Drift assumes decelerating growth from +92% YoY toward the low double digits by 2030 as the market matures and custom ASICs (TPU, Trainium, MTIA) take share. Left tail is a demand air-pocket plus share loss; right tail is continued near-monopoly on the merchant accelerator market.

continuous_variables.name: Combined annualized revenue run-rate, OpenAI + Anthropic
continuous_variables.notes: Current value uses OpenAI ~$25B (verified, mid-2026) plus Anthropic ~$47B (reported at the May 28 Series H; a $30B figure was also widely reported for April, so this input is uncertain by ~35%). Note the reporting basis is self-declared run-rate, not GAAP revenue, and may include related-party and credit-financed compute deals. Drift implies growth decelerating from ~150%/yr today toward ~25%/yr by 2031.

continuous_variables.name: Log2 of METR 50%-reliability task time horizon
continuous_variables.notes: Current value of 1.6 corresponds to ~3 hours — a compromise between the ~2h17m METR figure for GPT-5 (May 2026) and higher claims of ~14.5h; sources conflict badly and this is my least-confident input. Drift of 1.3 log2/yr equals a doubling every ~9 months, deliberately SLOWER than both the historical 7-month and the claimed recent 4-month doubling, because I expect the curve to bend as tasks get messier and less verifiable. p50 2031 of 8.1 is ~275 hours (~7 work-weeks); p10 is ~42 hours (one work-week); p90 is ~1800 hours (about a work-year).

continuous_variables.name: Log10 of API price for GPT-4-class capability
continuous_variables.notes: Current value of -0.4 is $0.40/Mtok for GPT-4-equivalent capability (verified: down from ~$20 in late 2022, a ~50x fall in 3.5 years). Drift of -0.28/yr equals a ~1.9x annual price decline, slower than the historical ~2.6x/yr because the easy gains (quantization, MoE, H100→B200) are largely banked and because memory/HBM and power costs are rising. p50 2031 of -1.8 is ~$0.016/Mtok. A floor around $0.003 (p10) reflects marginal electricity and HBM cost.

continuous_variables.name: Chinese open-weight models' share of OpenRouter tokens
continuous_variables.notes: Verified at ~61% as of May 2026, with 4 of the top 5 most-used models Chinese and Meta's Llama off the rankings entirely. Near-zero drift with high vol reflects genuine two-sidedness: US export controls or a Chinese-model security incident could collapse the share, while continued price aggression and Apache-2.0 licensing could push it toward 80%. Caveat: OpenRouter is a biased sample (price-sensitive developers), not the whole token market — enterprise volume runs direct to Anthropic/OpenAI/Google.

continuous_variables.name: Log10 of US paid fully-driverless rides per week (millions)
continuous_variables.notes: Current value of -0.3 is ~500k rides/week (verified, Waymo March 2026), with a stated target of 1M/week by end-2026. Drift of 0.24 log10/yr equals ~1.7x per year — deliberately below the recent ~4x/yr because vehicle manufacturing, depot capex, and per-city regulatory approval become binding as the base grows. p50 2031 of 0.9 is ~8M rides/week (~15% of US rideshare); p90 of 1.4 is ~25M/week. Left tail reflects a fatality-driven regulatory freeze.

continuous_variables.name: US AI adoption in production, employment-weighted (Census BTOS)
continuous_variables.unit: percent of employment at AI-using firms
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: BTOS shows 17-20% firm-weighted and ~32% employment-weighted use in production of goods/services (Nov 2025-May 2026), with firms expecting 22% within six months. Note BTOS uses a strict production-based definition and undercounts informal use. Growth is bounded above by the fact that 57% of adopters use AI in three or fewer functions — depth, not breadth, is the constraint. This variable is the best available leading indicator for AI's eventual measurable productivity and labor effects.

feedback_loops.name: Capability–revenue–capex–compute flywheel
feedback_loops.mechanism: Better models win enterprise contracts; revenue and equity appreciation fund larger clusters; larger clusters train better models. The verified numbers show all four stages simultaneously live: Nvidia data center +92% YoY, hyperscaler capex ~2x YoY, frontier lab ARR growing ~150%/yr, and monotone benchmark gains. This loop has driven the domain since 2022 and is the reason drift terms are positive almost everywhere.

feedback_loops.name: Grid and ratepayer backlash brake
feedback_loops.mechanism: Datacenter load drives capacity auction prices (PJM $28.92 → $329.17/MW-day, at the cap) which raise household bills (~$70/month projected by 2028), which produces political backlash (6+ states with moratorium bills, 7 restricting tax incentives, Oregon's dedicated rate class), which lengthens interconnection queues and raises the effective cost of new compute. This is currently the most underrated brake on the buildout because it operates through politics rather than markets.

feedback_loops.name: Jevons loop on inference cost
feedback_loops.mechanism: Inference cost per unit capability has fallen ~50x since 2022 ($20 → $0.40 per million tokens for GPT-4-class). Cheaper tokens make agentic workflows economical, agentic workflows consume 10-100x more tokens per task than chat, and aggregate token demand grows faster than unit price falls. This is why 'AI is getting cheap' has not reduced compute demand and probably will not.

feedback_loops.name: Export control → indigenous substitution
feedback_loops.mechanism: US controls on chips create guaranteed domestic demand and unlimited state funding for Chinese substitutes; the July 2026 start of domestic immersion DUV mass production (Shanghai Aishengna, absorbing SMEE and Yuliangsheng/SiCarrier teams) is the clearest evidence yet. Each round of controls buys time but permanently reduces future leverage. Beijing's refusal to buy licensed H200s is the deliberate policy expression of this loop.

feedback_loops.name: Open-weight commoditization pressure
feedback_loops.mechanism: Chinese open-weight models at ~61% of OpenRouter tokens and within single digits of frontier on engineering benchmarks compress the price a closed lab can charge for mid-tier capability. This forces closed labs upmarket into the narrow band of hardest reasoning, shrinking the revenue base that must amortize $200M-$3B training runs. It is the main mechanism by which AI capex could be starved without any technical slowdown.

feedback_loops.name: AI accelerating AI R&D
feedback_loops.mechanism: Models now write a large share of kernel optimizations, chip-design RTL, training-infrastructure code, and increasingly research ideation; METR's rising time horizon is exactly the metric that governs how much of the research loop can be delegated. If this crosses a threshold it becomes the dominant term in the whole model, invalidating extrapolation from historical scaling rates in the fast direction.

feedback_loops.name: Capital-markets reflexivity and circular financing
feedback_loops.mechanism: Equity valuations fund capex; capex is booked as revenue by suppliers and partners (vendor financing, equity-for-compute swaps, Oracle/OpenAI-style multi-year prepay structures); that revenue supports valuations. Moody's ~$662B of signed-but-not-commenced lease commitments sits off balance sheet. The loop runs equally hard in reverse — the July 28 Nasdaq correction is the reverse gear engaging.

feedback_loops.name: Incident → regulation → deployment friction
feedback_loops.mechanism: Misuse events (GTG-1002 AI-orchestrated espionage; jailbreak claims triggering the June 12 BIS directive against Fable 5/Mythos 5) produce regulatory response, which raises compliance and legal cost and slows deployment. Currently weak — the June directive was reversed in 18 days and the EU delayed high-risk obligations by 16 months — but it strengthens sharply after any event with visible casualties.

feedback_loops.name: Displacement → political constraint on automation
feedback_loops.mechanism: Entry-level displacement (22-25yo software developer employment -20% since 2024) concentrated in politically articulate cohorts feeds AI-skeptical politics, which raises the probability of licensing regimes, automation taxes, or sectoral restrictions. Slow-acting and currently latent because aggregate unemployment shows no AI effect, but the November 2026 midterms are the first electoral test.

structural_uncertainties: Measurement collapse: there is no agreed capability metric that survives saturation. MMLU is dead, HLE is at 53%, ARC-AGI-2 is at 85% while ARC-AGI-3 is under 1%, and METR's time-horizon figures differ by 6x across sources I searched this session. Every capability-conditioned probability in this model inherits that ambiguity, and 'AGI' questions may be permanently unresolvable rather than merely uncertain.

Revenue figures are not audited. OpenAI and Anthropic 'run-rate' numbers are self-declared, non-GAAP, and reported inconsistently (Anthropic $30B vs $47B within six weeks). If a material fraction of AI revenue is circular — compute vendors funding customers who buy their compute, equity-for-capacity swaps, related-party prepays — then the true demand base could be 30-50% smaller than headline, and the entire capex model is built on a mismeasured foundation.

Recursive self-improvement discontinuity. If AI systems begin contributing the majority of frontier AI research, the drift terms here become meaningless: compute-efficiency gains, not compute scaling, would drive capability, and 2031 deciles would be wrong by orders of magnitude in the fast direction. Nothing in the current data distinguishes 'agents are useful research assistants' from 'the takeoff has quietly started'.

Symmetric plateau risk. Reasoning gains since 2024 came largely from RL on verifiable tasks. If verifiable-task supply is the binding input, capability could flatten abruptly in domains without cheap verification (most of the economy), while benchmarks keep rising. This would make the METR curve a measure of benchmark engineering rather than autonomy, and would break every labor and revenue projection here in the slow direction.

Financial contagion is the fastest-acting unmodeled channel. Datacenter buildout is increasingly financed through private credit, SPVs, and off-balance-sheet leases (~$662B signed-but-not-commenced per Moody's). A credit event would cut compute growth far faster and more discontinuously than any technical or physical constraint, and would propagate into domains this model treats as exogenous.

Taiwan. Every number in this model — CoWoS at 120-140k wafers/month, TSMC 2nm allocation, HBM supply, Nvidia's entire product line — routes through a single island under active military coercion. A blockade or invasion would not perturb these forecasts; it would replace the domain with a different one. I have deliberately excluded this from the discrete risks because it belongs to the geopolitics domain, but it dominates the joint distribution.

The binding constraint keeps moving and I cannot predict the sequence. It has been GPUs (2023), then advanced packaging (2024-25), now power and grid interconnection (2026), with transformers, HV switchgear, skilled electricians, water rights, and turbine lead times each plausibly next. Models that assume a single stable bottleneck systematically underestimate delay.

Model weight security. All diffusion assumptions here — the China-US gap, the open-vs-closed gap, misuse probabilities — collapse if frontier weights are stolen or leaked. The June 2026 BIS directive against Fable 5/Mythos 5 shows the US government now treats weights as controllable artifacts, which implies they believe exfiltration matters; there is no public evidence about how well labs are actually defending them against state actors.

research.state_of_play:
As of July 2026 the world holds roughly 8.30 billion people and global TFR is around 2.23 (UN WPP 2024 medium variant baseline; the 2026 WPP revision had not appeared in my searches as of this session — UN DESA has published a "World Population Highlights 2026: Youth" brief but I could NOT verify a full 2026 revision, so all UN-projection statements here rest on WPP 2024, which puts the global peak at ~10.3bn in 2084).

Three verified shocks define H1 2026. First, China's demographic decline sharply accelerated. NBS data released 19 January 2026 showed 2025 births of 7.92 million — down 1.62m (-17%) from the dragon-year 2024 figure of 9.54m and the lowest of the modern era. Deaths rose to 11.31m; population fell 3.39m to 1.405bn, the fourth consecutive and largest annual decline (2022 -0.85m, 2023 -2.08m, 2024 -1.39m). Q1 2026 marriage registrations hit a record low of 1.697m, -6.2% y/y and less than half the 2017 level, which forecloses any 2026-27 birth rebound. Beijing's response is real but small: a national childcare subsidy of RMB3,600/child/year under age 3 reached 25.16 million babies by July 2026, funded with RMB99.9bn central (~RMB110bn total, roughly 0.08% of GDP), with a "birth-friendly society" written into the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030).

Second, the rich-world migration regime inverted. US net international migration collapsed: AEI and Brookings' January 2026 update estimates 2025 net migration between -295,000 and roughly zero, the first non-positive year in at least half a century; Census's own Vintage series showed NIM halving to 1.26m for the year to July 2025 and projected only ~321,000 to July 2026. The FY2026 refugee ceiling was set at 7,500, an all-time low, and a December 2025 proclamation barred family sponsorship from 39 countries; the $100,000 H-1B entry fee remains in litigation. On 30 June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that the 14th Amendment does guarantee birthright citizenship, closing that avenue. In the UK, ONS reported on 21 May 2026 that net migration fell to 171,000 in the year to December 2025, from 331,000 and a 2023 peak of 944,000. In the EU, asylum applications fell 19% in 2025 to 822,000 (lowest since 2021), and the Pact on Migration and Asylum became fully applicable on 12 June 2026, locking in mandatory border procedures, an EU safe-country list, and faster returns.

Third, and genuinely counter-narrative: forced displacement fell for the first time in a decade. UNHCR reported (June 2026) 117.8 million forcibly displaced at end-2025, with refugees down 3% to 41.6m and 14.7m returns during 2025 (4.4m refugees, 10.3m IDPs) — the second-highest refugee-return total on record, driven by Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan. Much of this is coerced, not voluntary: Iran and Pakistan expelled ~3.6m Afghans in early 2026 (5.4m since October 2023), and the UN expects ~3.2m returns to Afghanistan in 2026 into a country where ~22m need humanitarian aid.

Other verified points: US 2025 provisional births 3,606,400 (-1%), general fertility rate 53.1/1,000 — a record low back to 1909; teen birth rate 11.7 (-7%). US overdose deaths fell ~14% to 69,973 in 2025, the third straight decline, and the crude death rate (~689/100k) was the lowest ever recorded, with life expectancy on track for a record high. Japan's 2025 births fell for a 10th straight year to 705,809 including foreign nationals (~670,000 Japanese nationals), with record natural decline of 899,845. Italy recorded ~355,000 births (-3.9%), TFR 1.14, natural decline -297,000 — yet its population stabilized at 58.94m on 1 Jan 2026 for the first time in 12 years, entirely on net migration. South Korea is the one bright spot: TFR rose a second year to 0.80 with births +6.8% to 254,500. India's SRS 2024 (released mid-2026) put TFR at 1.9, a fifth consecutive sub-replacement year; Census 2027 houselisting is running April-September 2026 with population enumeration referenced to 1 March 2027. Africa's median age is 19.5; up to 12m youth enter the labor market yearly against ~3m formal salaried jobs created. I did not verify Germany's 2025 vital statistics or US 2025 final life-expectancy figures and treat them as inferred.
