discrete_risks.name: China annual births fall below 7.0 million
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: China's National Bureau of Statistics reports annual births below 7,000,000 for any calendar year, in its regular January statistical communique or the annual Statistical Yearbook.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2025 births were 7.92m. The cohort of women aged 20-34 is shrinking roughly 3-4% per year through the mid-2030s as the 1990s birth collapse ages in. Q1 2026 marriages fell another 6.2% to a record low, and marriage leads births by 1-2 years in China where non-marital births are rare. 2026 is also a fire-horse zodiac year. A 12% cumulative decline over 2026-27 is close to the central path, not a tail.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: annual births in China over the last decade. 2016 17.86m, 2019 14.65m, 2021 10.62m, 2022 9.56m, 2023 9.02m, 2024 9.54m, 2025 7.92m. Six of the last nine years saw declines exceeding 6%; the mean annual change 2016-2025 is about -8%.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: 2024 showed births can rise 6% on zodiac and post-COVID marriage catch-up. The 2026-2030 subsidy regime (RMB3,600/child, free childbirth in 28 provinces, possible expansion in the 15th Five-Year Plan) could deliver a 5-10% level shift, and Korea has now posted two consecutive TFR increases, showing ultra-low-fertility East Asian societies are not monotonic. If Beijing escalates to genuinely large cash transfers, 7m could be defended for several years.

discrete_risks.name: China's officially reported population falls below 1.400 billion
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NBS reports a year-end national population (mainland, excluding HK/Macau/Taiwan) below 1,400 million.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Year-end 2025 was 1.405bn with a -3.39m annual change that is accelerating as the large 1962-1975 cohorts enter high-mortality ages while births fall. Only ~5m of further decline is required. A 2026 decline of 4-5m plus any 2027 decline clears the threshold; the main uncertainty is whether 2026 alone suffices and whether NBS rounding presents 1.400 or 1.401.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: annual declines since the 2022 turning point — 0.85m, 2.08m, 1.39m, 3.39m. Mean -1.93m, most recent -3.39m and trending steeper. Deaths have exceeded 10.9m every year since 2022 and are structurally rising.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: NBS annual figures are model-based sample extrapolations, not counts, and the agency has political incentives to smooth a symbolically loaded threshold. Mortality could also mean-revert downward after the 2023 COVID-exit excess, and a subsidy-driven birth uptick plus slower deaths could stretch the crossing past 2027. There is also a real chance NBS simply revises the series at the 2030 census rather than crossing gradually.

discrete_risks.name: Japan annual births (Japanese nationals) fall below 600,000
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Japan's MHLW Vital Statistics report annual births to Japanese nationals below 600,000 for any calendar year, in preliminary or final figures.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2025 was roughly 670,000 Japanese-national births (705,809 including foreign nationals, -2.1%), the tenth consecutive record low. The base needs to fall about 10.5%. 2026 is hinoeuma (fire horse), a superstition that cut Japanese births ~25% in 1966; even a muted 5-8% modern effect plus the underlying 2-4% trend would put 2026 near or below 600k, with a partial 2027 rebound.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Japanese annual births 2015-2025 fell from 1.006m to ~0.670m, an average of -3.9% per year, with -5.7% in 2024. Reaching 600k requires roughly 2.5 average years of decline. The 1966 hinoeuma precedent is a single observation but a very large one.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The 1966 hinoeuma effect operated in a society where arranged marriage and astrological matching were near-universal; contemporary Japanese couples largely ignore zodiac. The observed 2025 decline was only 2.1%, markedly slower than 2024's 5.7%, suggesting the post-COVID marriage recovery is feeding through. If that continues, 600k might not be breached until 2029-2030.

discrete_risks.name: US Census Bureau officially reports negative net international migration
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A Census Bureau Vintage population estimates release (or an official Census Bureau revision) reports negative net international migration for any 12-month estimating period.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Independent estimates (AEI, Brookings, January 2026) put 2025 net migration between -295,000 and roughly zero, but Census's own Vintage series recorded +1.26m to July 2025 and projected +321,000 to July 2026 — the agency's method leans on administrative and ACS-based residual approaches that lag and under-detect departures. Getting to a printed negative requires both continued policy restriction and a methodological update.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Census has published NIM every year since 1990 and never printed a negative annual figure — 0 for 36 observations. The lowest was roughly +250,000 in 2020-21 under complete border closure and a visa-processing halt.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Two symmetric errors are possible. Census may adopt a new departure-estimation methodology under an administration keen to document outflows, making a negative print more likely and sooner than the base rate suggests. Conversely, the political regime could reverse in January 2029, restoring inflows before the estimating machinery ever catches up, so the negative never gets printed at all.

discrete_risks.name: US total fertility rate falls below 1.50
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: CDC/NCHS reports a US total fertility rate below 1,500 births per 1,000 women (i.e. TFR < 1.50) for any calendar year, provisional or final.
discrete_risks.reasoning: US TFR was about 1.60 in 2024 and roughly 1.58 in 2025 (2025 GFR of 53.1 is a record low; births -1%). The trend since 2007 is about -1.2% per year with occasional flat years. Straight extrapolation reaches 1.50 around 2031-2033. The teen birth rate collapse (-7% in 2025 to 11.7) is largely exhausted as a source of further decline, which slows the trend; the main downward driver now is postponement among women in their twenties.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US TFR annual changes 2007-2025 — 2.12 to ~1.58, a 25% cumulative decline over 18 years, averaging -1.6%/yr with a brief 2021 rebound. No peer country that fell below 1.6 has returned above it durably (Germany, UK, Canada, Finland all continued down).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Sharply reduced immigration removes higher-fertility recent arrivals from the denominator in complicated ways, and could paradoxically raise measured TFR for the resident population. Federal pronatalist policy (expanded child credits, baby bonuses, IVF access) is now bipartisan-adjacent, and the US has a large religious high-fertility subpopulation that puts a firmer floor under national TFR than in East Asia or Southern Europe.

discrete_risks.name: Best-available global TFR estimate falls below 2.1
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A UN DESA World Population Prospects revision (or UN Population Division estimate) reports a global total fertility rate below 2.10 for the then-current year.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Global TFR is about 2.23 in 2026 on the WPP 2024 medium variant, which projects crossing 2.1 in the late 2040s. But actual outcomes have run below successive UN medium variants for a decade, most dramatically in China and now India (SRS 1.9). If the realized decline runs at the recent ~0.025-0.03/year rather than the projected ~0.015, crossing arrives in the mid-2030s. Africa's fertility, which holds up the global average, is falling faster than projected in Kenya, Ghana, Senegal and Ethiopia.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: every WPP revision since 2010 has revised the global TFR path downward and the peak-population year earlier (2100+ → 2086 → 2084). Six consecutive revisions in one direction is a strong prior for continued downward revision, though each individual step has been modest (2 years of peak-timing per revision).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The global average is dominated by Sub-Saharan Africa, where fertility decline has repeatedly stalled at 4-5 (Nigeria, Niger, DRC) and where data quality is poor enough that the UN's estimates could be too low or too high by 0.3. A stall — or, more mundanely, upward revision of African fertility after Nigeria finally holds a census — would push the crossing out past 2050.

discrete_risks.name: South Korea total fertility rate reaches 1.00 or above
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Statistics Korea reports an annual total fertility rate of 1.00 or higher for any calendar year.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Korea's TFR rose from 0.72 (2023) to 0.75 (2024) to 0.80 (2025), with 2025 births +6.8% to 254,500. Reaching 1.00 requires a further 25% rise. Statistics Korea attributes the recovery to a marriage rebound, a temporary bulge in the early-30s cohort, and attitude shifts. The early-30s cohort peaks around 2026-27 and then shrinks sharply, so the denominator turns hostile just as the tempo effect exhausts.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: national TFR recoveries from below 1.0. Only a handful of jurisdictions have ever recorded sub-1.0 TFR (Korea, Hong Kong, Macau, Singapore, Taiwan, some Eastern European cities in the 1990s). Eastern Europe did recover from ~1.1-1.2 to 1.5-1.6 over 15 years post-1999, but no national economy has climbed back above 1.0 from below 0.8 in under a decade — zero for the reference class so far.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The Eastern European precedent is genuinely encouraging: Russia, Czechia and Estonia all rose 30-40% from their late-1990s troughs once economic shock passed. Korea's rise is now two years old, is driven by a real 15%+ jump in marriages, and comes with an enormous policy push (housing, cash, corporate leave mandates). If a quarter of the deferred births of the 2015-2023 cohorts materialize, 1.0 is reachable by 2030.

discrete_risks.name: Global forced displacement exceeds 130 million
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: UNHCR Global Trends (or Mid-Year Trends) reports total forcibly displaced persons exceeding 130,000,000 at any reporting date.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Displacement peaked at 123.2m (end-2024) and fell to 117.8m at end-2025 — the first decline in a decade — driven by 14.7m returns to Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan. Reaching 130m requires a net +12m, i.e. a new conflict on the scale of Ukraine plus Sudan combined, or a reversal of the return wave. Aid-funding cuts also degrade UNHCR's ability to register and count, biasing reported totals down.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: annual changes in UNHCR total displacement 2015-2025 — roughly +3m, +2m, +3m, +2m, +9m (2021-22 Ukraine), +11m, +8m, -5m. Increases of 8m+ occurred in 3 of 10 years, always tied to a single named mega-crisis (Syria, Ukraine, Sudan).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The return wave may be a one-off drawdown of a Syria backlog rather than a trend; if Syria destabilizes again, or if Sudan's war spreads to Chad and South Sudan, or if a Sahel state collapses, displacement could add 10m in 18 months. Conversely, coerced returns from Iran and Pakistan mechanically reduce the refugee count without reducing human suffering, so this indicator may be measuring host-state policy more than conflict.

discrete_risks.name: EU return hubs operationalized at scale
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: At least three EU member states have transferred a cumulative total of 1,000 or more rejected asylum applicants or asylum seekers to designated 'return hubs' or processing centres in non-EU third countries under the Returns Regulation or bilateral arrangements, as documented by the European Commission, EUAA, or a major NGO monitor.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The Pact became fully applicable on 12 June 2026 with mandatory border procedures, an EU safe-country list, and a Return Border Procedure Regulation. The Commission's separate returns proposal explicitly contemplates third-country return hubs. Italy's Albania centres are the live template but have been repeatedly blocked by Italian and EU courts and have processed only handfuls of people. Scaling to 1,000+ across three states requires both willing third countries and courts standing down.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: externalized processing attempts by Western democracies — Australia (Nauru/Manus, ~4,000 transferred, succeeded), UK-Rwanda (0 transferred, killed by courts and change of government), Italy-Albania (dozens, repeatedly voided), Denmark-Rwanda (abandoned), Israel-Rwanda/Uganda (thousands, informal). Roughly 2 of 6 attempts reached meaningful scale, and the successful ones took 3-5 years.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The binding constraint has never been EU legislation; it is that no capable third country will accept non-nationals at scale without payments that dwarf domestic detention costs, and that the ECtHR and CJEU keep voiding the arrangements. Five years of political will has produced almost zero transfers. The honest base case may be that this remains permanently symbolic.

discrete_risks.name: A G7 country cuts permanent immigration by three quarters
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A G7 member's official annual permanent-residence/settlement admissions (e.g. US lawful permanent residents, Canada PR admissions, UK settlement grants) fall below 25% of that country's 2024 level for a full fiscal or calendar year, per the responsible national agency.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Restriction so far has hit flows that are executive-discretionary — refugees (US FY2026 cap 7,500, a 95%+ cut), humanitarian parole, student dependants, care-worker visas. Permanent family and employment immigration is statutory and much harder to cut: the US issues ~1m green cards a year under numerical caps set by Congress. The December 2025 proclamation barring family sponsorship from 39 countries is a partial move in this direction and survives judicial review only partly. Canada has already cut PR targets ~20%.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: 75%+ multi-year cuts in permanent immigration by wealthy democracies. The US 1924 Johnson-Reed Act (achieved ~80% cut, held for 40 years) and the 1930s administrative shutdown are the only clean precedents in a century — roughly 2 events in 100 country-decades for the G7, implying a base rate near 1-2% per country-decade before adjusting upward for current politics.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Business lobbies, hospital systems, agriculture and universities in every G7 country have blocked exactly this for fifty years, and the labor-shortage pressure from aging is intensifying, not easing. Canada already partially reversed its cuts under employer pressure. Also, the more effective restriction is enforcement and processing throughput, not statutory caps — governments can achieve the political benefit without ever passing the law, which makes this specific resolution criterion unlikely to trigger.

discrete_risks.name: Youth-led protests topple three or more Sub-Saharan African governments in a three-year window
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: In any rolling 36-month window, heads of state or heads of government in three or more Sub-Saharan African countries resign, are removed, or flee within 90 days of the onset of mass protests that contemporaneous major-outlet reporting characterizes as youth-led or 'Gen Z' protests.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Africa's median age is 19.5 and up to 12m young people enter the labor market annually against ~3m formal salaried jobs; 61% of NEET youth are women and only 9% complete tertiary education. The 2024-2025 wave (Kenya's finance-bill protests, Nigeria's #EndBadGovernance, Mozambique, Madagascar's successful Gen Z uprising) shows the mechanism is live and is propagating through social media across borders. But protests toppling governments remains rare relative to protests occurring.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: SSA leaders removed within 90 days of mass protest onset, 2010-2025 — Burkina Faso 2014 (Compaoré), Sudan 2019 (Bashir, via military), Madagascar 2025. Roughly 3 in 16 years across ~48 countries, i.e. about 0.19/year continent-wide. Three in a 36-month window requires a rate 5x the historical average, which is what a genuine wave looks like (cf. Arab Spring 2011: 4 in 12 months).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Most SSA incumbents facing youth protest have survived: Ruto, Tinubu, Museveni, and the Sahel juntas all absorbed 2024-25 waves with repression and cosmetic concessions. Toppling requires elite defection or military neutrality, which coalitions of unemployed urban youth rarely secure. The pattern is more likely persistent low-grade unrest and emigration pressure than serial regime change, which is arguably worse for outcomes but does not resolve this question yes.

discrete_risks.name: PISA 2025 shows no recovery in OECD-average mathematics
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: OECD PISA 2025 results report an OECD-average mathematics score equal to or below the PISA 2022 OECD-average mathematics score (472 points).
discrete_risks.reasoning: Resolves at the September/December 2026 release. PISA 2022 recorded the largest single-cycle drop in the programme's history (-15 points in math). The 2025 cohort was aged 8-9 during peak school closures, so it absorbed disruption at the foundational-numeracy stage. Post-COVID recovery evidence from NAEP, national assessments in England, Germany and the Netherlands is weak to negative, and secular pre-COVID decline was already underway from 2012 in most OECD systems. Smartphone/attention effects are unmeasured but plausibly negative.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: OECD-average math across PISA cycles — 2003 500, 2006 494, 2009 496, 2012 494, 2015 490, 2018 489, 2022 472. Six of seven inter-cycle changes were declines; the mean change is about -4.7 points per cycle. Simple trend extrapolation predicts ~467, i.e. below 472.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Some of the 2022 drop was a pure testing-conditions artifact (many countries assessed during disrupted schooling), so a mechanical bounce-back is plausible. Composition also matters: several high-performing East Asian and Gulf systems have expanded participation and improved, and OECD averages are sensitive to which countries are in the OECD-average basket. Sharp national recoveries in Japan, Korea, Singapore and Ireland could carry the average up a few points.

discrete_risks.name: US life expectancy at birth reaches 80.0 years
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NCHS reports US period life expectancy at birth of 80.0 years or more for a single calendar year, in final or provisional mortality reports.
discrete_risks.reasoning: US mortality is improving faster than at any point since the 1970s: overdose deaths fell ~14% in 2025 to 69,973 (third consecutive decline), the crude death rate hit a record low ~689/100k, and NCHS reported life expectancy on track for a record high. GLP-1 uptake at population scale plausibly adds meaningfully to cardiometabolic mortality improvement over the next decade. From roughly 79.3-79.5 today, reaching 80.0 needs 0.5-0.7 years — one good half-decade.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US life expectancy trajectory — 78.9 (2014 pre-decline peak), 78.8 (2019), 77.0 (2020), 76.4 (2021), 77.5 (2022), 78.4 (2023), ~79.3 (2024). Recovery years have run +0.9/yr but that is rebound, not trend. The long-run US pre-2010 trend was about +0.15/yr, which would need 4 years from 79.3.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The current gains are rebound plus a fentanyl-supply shock (reduced potency of the street supply) that could reverse. The US has structural mortality problems — firearms, motor vehicles, obesity, uninsurance, midlife cardiometabolic disease — that stalled life expectancy at 78.9 for six years pre-COVID with no obvious remedy. Medicaid coverage losses and public health funding cuts push the other way. It is entirely possible the US plateaus at 79.5.

discrete_risks.name: China's population is revised down by 15 million or more
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: An official Chinese government source (NBS communique, the 2030 national census, or a published statistical yearbook revision) reports a national population figure at least 15,000,000 below the previously published estimate for a comparable date.
discrete_risks.reasoning: China's inter-censal figures are sample-survey extrapolations. Independent demographers (Yi Fuxian most prominently) argue local incentives to inflate headcounts for fiscal transfers and school allocations have produced a cumulative overcount possibly exceeding 100m, concentrated in birth cohorts from the one-child era. The 2030 census (reference date 1 November 2030) is the forcing event; the 2020 census, however, produced an upward surprise rather than a downward one.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Chinese census-driven revisions. The 2000 census implied undercount corrections upward; 2010 and 2020 both resulted in figures at or above prior estimates. Zero of three recent censuses produced a large downward revision. Elsewhere, Nigeria (2006) and Indonesia have produced large revisions, but usually upward.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The strongest argument against is simply the track record: every Chinese census in living memory has revised the population up, not down, because the incentive at the household level is to hide extra children under the one-child policy, not to invent them. The overcount thesis rests heavily on school-enrolment comparisons that have alternative explanations. And even if a discrepancy exists, NBS has strong political reasons to smooth it across years rather than book it in one release.

discrete_risks.name: India publishes provisional Census 2027 population totals
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India publishes provisional population totals from Census 2027, covering the population enumeration phase with a reference date of 1 March 2027.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Phase I houselisting is running April-September 2026 under a formal notification issued January 2026; population enumeration is referenced to 1 March 2027. In 2011, provisional totals were released on 31 March 2011, one month after enumeration — so a within-2027 release is achievable. Against that: this census is fully digital and self-enumeration-enabled for the first time, includes caste enumeration for the first time since 1931, and India already slipped this census by six years. Caste tabulation is politically explosive and could delay any release.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Indian decennial censuses since 1881 — 15 conducted, all completed on schedule with provisional totals within roughly one to two months of enumeration, except 2021, which was postponed six years. So 14 of 15 delivered on time, but the single failure is the most recent one.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The delimitation stakes are enormous: an accurate count redistributes Lok Sabha seats from low-fertility southern states to high-fertility northern ones, and southern chief ministers have explicitly campaigned against it. Combined with the caste count, there is a serious political incentive to complete the enumeration but sit on the results past the 2029 general election. Untested digital infrastructure at 1.46bn scale is a further failure mode.

discrete_risks.name: China's direct birth and childcare subsidies reach 0.5% of GDP
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Combined central and local government direct cash transfers for childbirth and childcare in China exceed 0.5% of nominal GDP in a single fiscal year, per Ministry of Finance budget documents or credible reporting aggregating central and provincial outlays.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The 2026 programme is RMB99.9bn central plus local, ~RMB110bn total, or roughly 0.08% of GDP — meaningful as a first move but an order of magnitude below what Hungary (~3-5% of GDP on family policy) or France spends. Reaching 0.5% means ~RMB700bn+. The 15th Five-Year Plan has committed rhetorically to a 'birth-friendly society', and 28 provinces have eliminated inpatient childbirth out-of-pocket costs. Escalation would require accepting that the current dose failed, which the 2026-27 birth data will make plain.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: countries that escalated pronatalist cash spending above 0.5% of GDP after crossing TFR 1.2 — Hungary (yes, within ~6 years), Korea (yes, on a broad definition, ~1%+), Russia (yes, maternity capital ~0.5%), Singapore (no), Japan (partially, on a broad definition). Roughly 3 of 5 escalated within a decade of the political salience threshold, though effect sizes on TFR were small (0.05-0.2).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: China's fiscal position is strained by local government debt, property-sector losses, and a rising pension bill that already dwarfs family policy; the leadership has consistently preferred supply-side and exhortative measures over large transfers to households. It may also read the Korean and Hungarian evidence correctly — that cash buys very little fertility — and choose to spend on eldercare and automation instead. The plausible path is expansion to 0.15-0.25% of GDP, not 0.5%.

continuous_variables.name: Global total fertility rate
continuous_variables.notes: WPP 2024 medium variant basis for the current value; realized outcomes have run below every UN medium variant for a decade, so the drift here is slightly steeper than UN's implied ~-0.015/yr. Downside skew is real: the tail risk is an unexpectedly fast African decline, not a rebound.

continuous_variables.name: China annual births
continuous_variables.notes: Verified 2025 NBS figure. Drift is dominated by the shrinking 20-34 female cohort (about -3.5%/yr), partly offset by the new subsidy regime. Vol is high because zodiac years (2026 fire horse, 2036 dragon) and marriage-cohort timing produce 10%+ single-year swings in both directions.

continuous_variables.name: US total fertility rate
continuous_variables.notes: Inferred from verified 2025 provisional GFR of 53.1 and births of 3,606,400. The teen-birth channel is nearly exhausted as a source of decline; the remaining driver is postponement in the twenties. Immigration composition effects add uncertainty in both directions.

continuous_variables.name: Global forcibly displaced persons
continuous_variables.notes: Verified UNHCR end-2025 figure, first decline in a decade. Distribution is right-skewed: new mega-conflicts add 8-11m in a year while declines are gradual, so treat the upside tail as fatter than a normal. Aid-funding cuts also degrade registration and bias reported totals downward.

continuous_variables.name: US net international migration
continuous_variables.notes: Current value is the Census Bureau's projection for the year to July 2026; independent estimates for calendar 2025 range from -295k to roughly zero. This is the single highest-variance variable in the domain — it is set almost entirely by US executive policy, so model it as regime-switching around the November 2028 election rather than as a smooth diffusion.

continuous_variables.name: EU+ annual asylum applications
continuous_variables.notes: Verified EUAA 2025 figure, -19% y/y and lowest since 2021. The Pact's border procedures and safe-country list push down; a Sahel, Maghreb or renewed Syrian/Ukrainian crisis pushes up sharply. Historic range 2014-2025 spans 200k to 1.4m, so vol should stay wide.

continuous_variables.name: India total fertility rate
continuous_variables.notes: Verified SRS 2024 value published mid-2026, fifth consecutive sub-replacement year. Base year is 2024, so 2031 is seven years of drift. Census 2027 could force a discontinuous revision if SRS sampling has drifted from reality. Northern high-fertility states (Bihar ~2.9) are the source of remaining decline headroom.

continuous_variables.name: World population
continuous_variables.notes: Near-deterministic over five years because it is dominated by momentum from cohorts already born. Almost all the uncertainty is measurement error, not demographic surprise — chiefly whether Nigeria, DRC and Ethiopia are counted anywhere near correctly. Annual increment is itself declining by about 1.5m/yr.

continuous_variables.name: China population aged 60 and over
continuous_variables.notes: Inferred forward from the verified 21.1% end-2023 figure (296.97m). Extremely low variance: everyone who will be 60+ in 2031 is already 55+ today, so only mortality surprises move it. The 1962-1975 baby boom cohorts are now crossing 60 at ~25m/yr, which is why the drift is steep.

continuous_variables.name: US annual drug overdose deaths
continuous_variables.notes: Verified CDC 2025 provisional figure of 69,973, down ~14% from 81,313. Recent declines are partly attributable to reduced street fentanyl potency, which is a supply-side condition that can reverse abruptly — hence a fat right tail. Regional divergence is stark (Northeast down 25%+, Southwest up 10%+).

continuous_variables.name: South Korea total fertility rate
continuous_variables.notes: Verified Statistics Korea 2025 figure, second consecutive rise. The world's most important natural experiment in whether ultra-low fertility is a floor or a trapdoor. Positive drift reflects the current marriage rebound, but the early-30s cohort shrinks sharply after 2027, so drift should decay toward zero in the 2030s.

continuous_variables.name: Japan annual births (Japanese nationals)
continuous_variables.notes: Approximate Japanese-national count for 2025 (705,809 including foreign nationals, verified, -2.1%). 2026 is hinoeuma (fire horse); the 1966 analogue cut births ~25%, so add a one-off negative shock in 2026 with partial reversal in 2027 if modelling year by year. Actual births have run 15+ years ahead of the 2023 IPSS official projection.

feedback_loops.name: Low-fertility trap
feedback_loops.mechanism: Fewer births today mean fewer potential mothers in twenty years, so the same TFR yields fewer births each generation. Simultaneously, small families become the observed social norm, child-oriented infrastructure (schools, pediatrics, playgrounds, family housing stock) contracts and raises the practical cost of the third child, and firms stop designing products and workplaces around parents. Korea, Italy and China are all inside this loop; only Korea shows any sign of resisting it.

feedback_loops.name: Migration substitution
feedback_loops.mechanism: Natural decrease creates labor scarcity, which raises wages and political pressure for immigration, which offsets population decline. Italy is the pure case: 355,000 births against 652,000 deaths in 2025, yet population stabilized at 58.94m on net migration of +296,000. This loop is what has kept Western Europe, Canada and Australia from shrinking, and it is currently being switched off by politics rather than by economics.

feedback_loops.name: Restriction backlash spiral
feedback_loops.mechanism: Visible migration raises salience, which elects restrictionists, who cut legal pathways. Cutting legal pathways diverts flows into irregular channels that are more visible and less controllable, raising salience further. Meanwhile the labor scarcity created by restriction generates a shadow labor market whose existence is then cited as evidence that enforcement has failed. The UK is the cleanest example: net migration fell 82% from its 2023 peak to 171,000, yet 49% of the public believes it rose and only 16% know it fell.

feedback_loops.name: Aging fiscal squeeze
feedback_loops.mechanism: Rising old-age dependency shifts public spending toward pensions and health, crowding out family benefits, childcare and education, and raising the tax burden on the working-age population. That lowers the disposable income of prospective parents and pushes skilled young workers to emigrate, worsening the dependency ratio further. China's response — raising the retirement age from 2025 and contribution years from 2030 — is an attempt to damp this loop rather than escape it.

feedback_loops.name: Automation substitution
feedback_loops.mechanism: Labor scarcity raises the relative price of labor, which pulls forward capital deepening, robotics and AI adoption, so output per worker rises fast enough to offset a shrinking workforce. Japan and Korea have the world's highest robot densities for exactly this reason. Note the sign can flip: if AI destroys entry-level and clerical work faster than it substitutes for scarce labor, young-adult income insecurity rises and household formation falls further, converting this into a reinforcing depopulation loop.

feedback_loops.name: Housing cost and delayed household formation
feedback_loops.mechanism: Concentration of jobs in expensive metros raises the housing cost of family formation, delaying marriage and first births. Delayed births produce an older electorate whose wealth is in housing, which then blocks supply expansion, sustaining the cost. China's Q1 2026 marriage registrations at 1.697m — less than half the 2017 level — and Korea's pre-2024 collapse both run through this channel; Korea's partial recovery followed an aggressive housing-and-cash package.

feedback_loops.name: Displacement and coerced return cycle
feedback_loops.mechanism: Host-state fatigue and funding cuts trigger mass returns, which mechanically reduce displacement counts. But absorption capacity in origin countries is far below the return volume, so returnees become internally displaced or re-migrate. Afghanistan is the live case: ~3.6m expelled from Iran and Pakistan in early 2026, ~5.4m since October 2023, into a country where ~22m need humanitarian assistance. The loop balances the count while degrading conditions.

feedback_loops.name: Youth bulge and jobs gap
feedback_loops.mechanism: Up to 12 million young Africans enter the labor market annually against roughly 3 million formal salaried jobs created. Unemployed urban youth raise unrest risk, which deters the investment that would create jobs, and drives emigration of exactly the higher-skilled workers who would build absorptive capacity. Only 9% of African youth complete tertiary education, so the human-capital channel that broke this loop in East Asia is much weaker here.

structural_uncertainties: Whether ultra-low fertility has a floor at all. Every projection in this domain, including the UN's, assumes mean reversion of TFR toward roughly 1.6-1.8 in the very-low-fertility countries. If that assumption is simply wrong — if there is no floor and Korea's 0.8 is a waypoint rather than a trough — then peak population arrives decades earlier and every dependency-ratio and pension model in existence is optimistic. Conversely, if Korea's two-year rise proves that most of the decline was tempo (postponement) rather than quantum (foregone births), a large mechanical rebound is coming and the depopulation literature is overshooting. These two possibilities are both live and imply opposite policy conclusions.

Population counts for roughly a fifth of humanity are essentially estimates. Nigeria's last census was 2006 and has been postponed repeatedly; DRC has not had one since 1984; Ethiopia's is long overdue. Africa's true population could plausibly be off by 10% in either direction, which flows straight into global TFR, global population, and every per-capita statistic. On the other side, China's inter-censal figures are sample extrapolations that some demographers argue overstate the population by tens of millions. The 2027 India census, the 2030 China census and the 2030 US census will all land inside the simulation horizon and could produce discontinuities larger than a decade of modelled drift.

The sign of the AI effect on demography is unknown, and it is probably the largest single unknown here. If AI substitutes for scarce labor, dependency ratios stop mattering, aging societies stay rich, and immigration demand collapses on the demand side rather than the political side. If AI instead eliminates the entry-level and clerical jobs that fund young-adult household formation, fertility falls further and faster in exactly the countries with the highest AI adoption. The current model treats automation as a balancing loop; it could be the strongest reinforcing loop in the system.

Migration is now set by politics on a two-to-four year cycle, not by economics on a generational one. The US swung from ~2.8m annual net migration in 2023-24 to something near zero or negative in 2025 with no change in wage or employment fundamentals. That means migration variables in this model are regime-switching processes driven by elections (US 2026, US 2028, EU national cycles) rather than diffusions, and any simulation that smooths them will systematically understate variance in labor supply, housing demand, and remittance flows.

Mortality could shift regime in either direction within the horizon. GLP-1 agonists at population scale plausibly add years to life expectancy in high-obesity countries over a decade — a mortality improvement with no modern precedent outside statins. Against that, antimicrobial resistance, a novel pandemic, or the reversal of the fentanyl-potency decline that drove the 2023-2025 US overdose fall could each remove a year or more. US life expectancy has already moved by ±2.5 years within a five-year window this decade, which no pre-2020 model would have permitted.

Definitional drift silently changes headline numbers. The UN's World Urbanization Prospects 2025 adopted the degree-of-urbanisation methodology and now reports 45% of people in 'cities' with 33 megacities and Jakarta at 42m — figures not comparable to the previous series. UNHCR's total includes UNRWA Palestine refugees and a growing 'other people in need of international protection' category. Census methodology for measuring emigration is under active revision in the US. Several of the indicators in this model could move by 5-15% through reclassification alone, and a naive simulation would read that as a real-world shock.

Composition and selection could put an unexpected floor under fertility. Within every low-fertility country, high-fertility religious and cultural subpopulations are growing as a share of the childbearing cohort — Haredi in Israel, Amish and conservative evangelicals in the US, Muslim communities in parts of Europe. If national TFR is a mixture of a collapsing majority and a stable high-fertility minority, the aggregate stops falling and then rises, on a timescale of 30-50 years, in a way that no linear extrapolation captures. This is a slow-moving structural effect that mostly sits past 2036 but shapes the terminal conditions of any long-horizon run.

Climate and conflict displacement could change character from internal and temporary to cross-border and permanent. Current displacement counts are dominated by conflict, and the 68.7m internally displaced are counted separately and treated as a distinct category. A sustained heat, water or crop-failure shock in South Asia, the Sahel or Central America that pushes displacement across borders at scale would break the conceptual boundary between 'migrant' and 'refugee' that all the institutional statistics rest on, and would arrive at precisely the moment when destination-country politics is least able to absorb it.

research.state_of_play:
The defining event of H1 2026 was the Iran crisis, which I verified this session. US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 Feb 2026 triggered an Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz, confirmed by the IRGC on 2 March; tanker transits collapsed and P&I insurance was withdrawn from ~5 March. The IEA characterised it as the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market, exceeding 1973. Brent ran from ~$75 to above $120 by April. A US-Iran ceasefire framework signed 17 June 2026 (a 60-day truce) included reopening the strait. The EIA's 7 July press release explicitly raised its global production forecast "after the opening of the Strait of Hormuz," and the July STEO cut full-year 2026 Brent by 14% to $82/bbl and 2027 by 18% to $65/bbl (Q3 2026 avg $74). Brent traded ~$72-74 in late July. Net: a four-month, historically unprecedented disruption that the system absorbed without industrial collapse, followed by a violent snap-back into an oversupplied market — roughly a 2 Mb/d surplus, OPEC+ proceeding with scheduled August increases, Goldman at $56 average for 2026. CAVEAT: several low-quality trackers still assert the strait is closed as of late July; I weight the EIA STEO revision and ceasefire reporting as authoritative and treat those trackers as stale or fabricated.

Underneath the shock, the structural story continued. IEA Global Energy Review 2026 (2025 data): solar PV generation rose 600 TWh, the largest single-year increase from any source outside post-crisis recovery; record 800 GW of renewable capacity additions, ~75% solar; solar supplied >25% of total energy demand growth — the first time a renewable led. Global coal-fired generation fell for the first time since 2019 (China -1.5%, India -3.0%), yet coal demand still grew 0.4% and energy CO2 hit a record >38 Gt. Electricity demand grew ~3% in 2025 and is forecast +3.7% in 2026; IEA Electricity 2026 expects power-sector emissions to plateau 2026-2030. Peak power-sector emissions is a live near-term claim; peak total fossil demand is not.

Risk has migrated to critical materials. IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: the average top-refiner share rose to 70% in 2025 (72% excluding rare earths), up not down; China holds >90% of gallium, graphite, manganese and rare earths and 60-90% of Li/Co/REE refining; ex-China graphite covers only ~10% of projected 2030 demand. Critical-minerals investment fell 9% in 2025. China's April 2025 REE licensing regime remains fully active, the 2026 catalogue added samarium, gadolinium and lutetium compounds, and in June 2026 China added MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to its control list. The October 2025 extraterritorial expansion is suspended only until 10 November 2026 — the single most consequential scheduled date in this domain. Meanwhile DRC replaced its cobalt export ban with a 96,600 t quota for 2026 (cobalt ~$26/lb, +160% off the Feb 2025 low), lithium spot rose ~180% between June 2025 and Feb 2026, and copper set record highs.

Electricity infrastructure is the binding OECD constraint. US interconnection queues exceed 2,600 GW; queue waits in Northern Virginia, Phoenix and Dallas run 4-7 years; GE Vernova's turbine book is sold into 2029-30 with turbine prices up ~195% versus 2019; large transformer lead times reach five years. US data-center consumption (183 TWh in 2024) is compounding 15-20%/yr. Europe's problem is price, not queue: EU industrial power is >2x US and ~50% above China, with network charges +46% since 2019.

US policy turned sharply against wind/solar: OBBBA set a 4 July 2026 begin-construction cliff for 45Y/48E with a 31 Dec 2027 placed-in-service backstop; a federal court restored the 5% safe harbor ahead of the deadline, producing a large H1 safe-harbor rush that will flatter 2026-27 installs and depress 2028+. Hydrogen has been marked to market: ~2.5 GW of electrolyzer capacity operational or under construction globally at end-Q1 2026 against a ~150 GW announced 2030 pipeline; ~60 projects (~4.9 Mtpa) cancelled in 2025. Nuclear is real but slow: 63 reactors under construction, uranium at 17-month highs ($83-85/lb in January), China's Linglong One due as the first land-based commercial SMR; no Western SMR before ~2029-30. Energy poverty: the 8 July 2026 SDG7 report counts 655 million without electricity and 2 billion without clean cooking, 86% of the gap in sub-Saharan Africa.

NOT VERIFIED this session (pre-2026 knowledge or inference): absolute global coal demand tonnage, OPEC+ effective spare capacity, TTF gas levels during the closure, China's 15th Five-Year Plan energy targets, and late-July copper/lithium spot levels.
