scheduled_events.name: US-Iran 60-day truce nominal expiry
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The ceasefire framework signed 17 Jun 2026 that reopened the Strait of Hormuz is time-limited. Non-renewal is the highest-probability near-term trigger for a repeat oil shock.

scheduled_events.name: OPEC+ August production tranche and subsequent ministerials
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: OPEC+ has signalled it will proceed with scheduled increases into an already ~2 Mb/d surplus, prioritising market share over price. Determines whether Brent breaks below $60.

scheduled_events.name: US midterm elections
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Determines whether the OBBBA clean-energy rollback is entrenched, softened or extended; also shapes FEOC enforcement and permitting-reform prospects.

scheduled_events.name: Expiry of China's 12-month suspension of expanded rare-earth export controls
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The single most consequential scheduled date in critical materials. Default absent action is snap-back of the October 2025 extraterritorial 0.1% de minimis regime, which would hit autos, defence, wind and robotics supply chains globally.

scheduled_events.name: COP31, Antalya, Turkey
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First COP assessing the full set of 2035 NDCs. Turkish presidency is pushing a '35 by 35' global electrification target (electricity to 35% of final energy from ~20%), which if adopted becomes a reference point for grid and power-sector investment.

scheduled_events.name: EU ETS2 launch for buildings and road transport
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Extends carbon pricing to households and transport fuels EU-wide. Politically explosive given the existing energy-cost backlash; delay or dilution is a live possibility and a bellwether for European climate-policy durability.

scheduled_events.name: IEA Global Energy Review 2027 (2026 data)
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: First authoritative read on whether the Hormuz shock permanently dented oil demand and whether global coal demand turned down.

scheduled_events.name: Qatar North Field South LNG startup
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Part of ~300 bcm/yr of new liquefaction to 2030 (half US, 20% Qatar). Deepens the structural LNG glut and caps European and Asian gas prices.

scheduled_events.name: OBBBA placed-in-service backstop for US wind and solar 45Y/48E credits
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Projects that safe-harboured before 4 Jul 2026 must be in service by this date or lose 30%+ tax credits. Creates a hard construction cliff and a probable 2028 US installation collapse.

scheduled_events.name: UNFCCC second Global Stocktake
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Formal assessment of collective progress; drives the 2035-2040 NDC cycle and the credibility of the tripling-renewables pledge.

scheduled_events.name: Darlington SMR (BWRX-300) Unit 1 targeted first power
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The lead Western SMR; OPG applied for its operating licence in March 2026. Success or slip sets the credibility of the whole OECD SMR pipeline and of nuclear as an AI-datacenter power source.

scheduled_events.name: TerraPower Natrium and X-energy/Dow Seadrift targeted operation
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Advanced-reactor demonstrations that also test the HALEU fuel supply chain, currently a Russian-legacy chokepoint.

scheduled_events.name: SDG7 universal energy access target year
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: Will be missed; IEA STEPS projects ~645 million still without electricity in 2030, 85% in sub-Saharan Africa. A quantified multilateral failure that shapes climate-finance politics.

scheduled_events.name: China 15th Five-Year Plan end and 2030 carbon-peak pledge horizon
scheduled_events.why_it_matters: China's trajectory dominates the global aggregate. Whether coal generation declines structurally over 2026-2030 determines whether global power-sector emissions have peaked.

discrete_risks.name: Strait of Hormuz closed again for 14+ consecutive days
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Commercial tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz fall below 25% of the 2025 daily average for 14 or more consecutive days, per Lloyd's List / Kpler / IEA Oil Market Report tracking, at any point after 1 Aug 2026.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The Feb-Jun 2026 closure demonstrated Iran will actually do it under existential military pressure, destroying the long-standing assumption that closure was a bluff. The ceasefire is a 60-day truce expiring ~16 Aug 2026, with the underlying nuclear dispute unresolved. Conditional on a renewed major US/Israel-Iran military exchange (which I put at ~35-40% by end-2027), closure probability is roughly 50-55% given revealed behaviour. Beyond 2027 the marginal hazard falls because Iran's export dependence on China and the reputational cost to Beijing make repetition costly, and because bypass infrastructure (Saudi East-West, ADNOC Fujairah) and SPR coordination will have been hardened.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: threatened closures of Hormuz since 1980 (Tanker War 1984-88, 2008, 2011-12, 2018-19, 2019 tanker attacks, 2024 Red Sea spillover, 2025 Israel-Iran war) - roughly 7 serious threat episodes in 46 years, exactly 1 actual closure. Unconditional base rate ~2%/yr; the 2026 event is strong evidence the true hazard was underestimated, so I roughly quadruple it and add near-term truce-expiry risk.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: my number is probably too high. The 2026 closure was catastrophic for Iran - it cut Iranian revenue, alienated China (its only major customer), and invited the strikes that forced the ceasefire. A rational Tehran treats it as a one-time card already played. If the June framework converts into a durable nuclear deal with sanctions relief, closure risk collapses toward the pre-2026 base rate and 24% by 2027 is roughly double what it should be. The market agrees with the sceptics: Brent at $72 with a 2 Mb/d surplus prices almost no closure premium.

discrete_risks.name: Brent monthly average above $120/bbl
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The calendar-month average of front-month Brent futures settlements exceeds $120.00/bbl (nominal USD) in any month after 1 Aug 2026, per ICE settlement data.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Even the largest supply disruption in oil history produced only a brief excursion above $120 in April 2026, not a sustained monthly average, because OECD stocks, OPEC+ idle capacity and a ~2 Mb/d structural surplus absorbed it. That is powerful evidence of system slack. Breaching a $120 monthly average requires either a longer Hormuz closure or simultaneous loss of a second major producer (Russia sanctions escalation, Venezuela, Nigeria, or an Abqaiq-class strike). Decelerating US shale growth and OPEC+ burning through spare capacity by the early 2030s raise the tail later in the horizon.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: months with Brent monthly average above $120 nominal since 1988 - roughly 12 months, all clustered in 2008 and Mar-Jun 2022. About 12 of ~460 months (2.6% of months), affecting ~15-20% of years but heavily clustered. Adjusting for the current surplus, near-term monthly hazard sits below the unconditional rate.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too low, especially at the long horizon. Nominal thresholds erode with inflation - $120 in 2036 is roughly $95 in today's money, so the 2036 figure should mechanically exceed a real-terms analysis. More importantly, OPEC+ is deliberately burning spare capacity to defend share; by 2029-2031 effective spare could fall below 2 Mb/d just as non-OPEC growth from Guyana, Brazil and US shale plateaus. A tight market plus any geopolitical event produces $120 easily, and 45-50% by 2031 is defensible.

discrete_risks.name: Brent monthly average below $45/bbl
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The calendar-month average of front-month Brent futures settlements falls below $45.00/bbl (nominal USD) in any month after 1 Aug 2026.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The market is in a ~2 Mb/d surplus with OPEC+ adding barrels to defend share rather than cutting. Goldman is at $56 for 2026 and EIA at $65 for 2027 - already close to the zone where a modest demand disappointment (global EV share 22.4% and rising, China at ~64% of domestic new car sales) or an OPEC+ discipline breakdown produces a genuine price war. The 2014-16 and 2020 analogues both had exactly this setup and both resolved into sub-$45 prints. Later in the horizon, structural oil demand peaking makes a share war more likely, not less, as producers race to monetise reserves.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: months with Brent monthly average below $45 nominal since 2005 - 2008-09 (about 5 months), 2016 (about 4 months), 2020 (about 5 months). Three episodes in 21 years, roughly 14%/yr episode hazard, with episodes concentrated in exactly the surplus conditions that presently obtain.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high. OPEC+ has repeatedly reversed course when prices threaten fiscal breakevens (Saudi needs ~$85-90); the 2026 market-share posture is a negotiating stance that historically lasts 6-18 months before cuts return. US shale is already rolling over (551 rigs, -25 y/y; Permian -12%) and responds to price within ~9 months, providing a floor around $50-55. Sub-$45 requires OPEC+ cohesion to actually break, which it never quite has.

discrete_risks.name: China's extraterritorial rare-earth export control regime enters into force
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The October 2025 expanded rare-earth export control measures (extraterritorial 0.1% de minimis provisions and expanded element list) are in legal force and being applied to licence applications for at least 30 consecutive days, per MOFCOM announcements, at any point before the stated year-end.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is a near-term scheduled binary: the suspension expires 10 Nov 2026 and the default absent action is snap-back. Beijing's revealed preference is to hold the regime as suspended leverage rather than spend it - the April 2025 licensing regime already gives granular control and is being enforced actively (2026 catalogue adding samarium, gadolinium, lutetium; June 2026 addition of MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to the control list). The modal outcome is another extension if the trade truce holds, but the truce is fragile and extension requires an affirmative diplomatic act, which is the harder path. Cumulative probability rises beyond 2027 as ex-China supply grows and the leverage depreciates, giving Beijing an incentive to use it before it decays.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Chinese export-control suspensions negotiated in US-China truces since 2018 - the 2019-20 Phase One truce, 2023 gallium/germanium (never suspended), 2024 antimony/graphite (never suspended), 2025 REE suspension. China has extended or maintained truce-linked suspensions roughly 60-65% of the time at decision points, but has never permanently withdrawn a control regime once written.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high for 2027. Both sides have strong incentives to keep the truce - the US needs REEs for defence and autos, China needs export markets amid weak domestic demand - and extensions of trade truces are the overwhelming historical norm because neither side wants to own the escalation. My resolution criterion is also demanding: China frequently lets a regime formally lapse into force while granting licences liberally, which would arguably not resolve YES on a strict reading of 'applied'. A 30% figure for 2027 is defensible.

discrete_risks.name: Severe rare-earth supply cutoff to the US or EU
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Chinese exports of NdPr oxide/metal or heavy rare earths (Dy, Tb) to either the United States or the European Union fall by more than 50% year-on-year for three or more consecutive months, per China customs data.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is the weaponisation scenario rather than the licensing-friction scenario. It requires a serious geopolitical rupture - Taiwan crisis, semiconductor export-control escalation, or defence-industrial confrontation. The April-June 2025 episode showed China will throttle to the point of shutting European auto lines but stops short of formal embargo, because a true cutoff accelerates exactly the substitution and onshoring it wants to prevent (ferrite and rare-earth-free motors, MP Materials, Lynas, recycling). Rising through the horizon as Taiwan tensions and semiconductor controls compound, then decaying late as ex-China supply materialises.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Chinese resource-export coercion episodes - 2010 Japan REE embargo (the only clear precedent, ~2 months), 2023 gallium/germanium (exports to US fell over 90% but from a small base), 2024 graphite/antimony controls, 2025 REE licensing squeeze. Roughly 4 coercion episodes in 16 years, only 1 reaching over 50% sustained cutoff to a major economy: about 6%/yr for the severe variant.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: uncertain, but the estimate is strongly correlated with Taiwan tail risk in a way the standalone number hides. Argument I am too low: China has already listed US rare-earth companies as sanctions targets (June 2026), signalling it treats this as a hard-security rather than trade domain, and in a Taiwan contingency a >50% cutoff is near-automatic. Argument I am too high: the 2010 Japan episode is the classic cautionary tale in Beijing - it triggered a decade of diversification and cost China permanent market share, and Chinese strategists explicitly cite it as a mistake.

discrete_risks.name: Cyberattack causes a major OECD power outage
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A cyber intrusion causes loss of electricity supply to 500,000 or more customers for 6 or more hours in an OECD member country, with cyber causation publicly confirmed by the relevant national CERT, regulator or system operator.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Threat activity is clearly escalating: the December 2025 attack on the Polish grid attributed to Berserk Bear notably targeted both IT and physical industrial devices, the precursor signature for the Ukraine 2015/2016 class of attack, and Volt Typhoon-style pre-positioning in US critical infrastructure is documented. But OECD grids have far more redundancy, manual fallback and post-2015 OT segmentation than the Ukrainian grid, and the largest confirmed cyber-caused outage in history remains 225,000 customers for a few hours. Crossing 500,000-for-6-hours in an OECD country would be a genuine first, most likely as a component of open interstate conflict rather than in peacetime.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: confirmed cyber-caused electricity outages globally 2010-2026 - Ukraine 2015 (225k, ~6h), Ukraine 2016 (Kyiv, ~1h), Ukraine 2022 Industroyer2 (blocked). Zero in OECD countries in ~16 years despite thousands of intrusion attempts. Unconditional OECD base rate below 2%/yr; I adjust upward for demonstrated pre-positioning and the Polish precedent.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: too low on the physics, too high on resolvability. Too low because grid digitisation, inverter-based resources with remote firmware update paths, and cloud-connected DER aggregators have massively expanded the attack surface since 2015 - an attack on inverter fleets bypasses all the substation-focused OT hardening built for the Ukraine threat model, and compromising one major inverter vendor's update channel could trip multiple GW. Too high because attribution is slow and contested: many outages with plausible cyber causes get officially attributed to equipment failure, so 'publicly confirmed' may never resolve YES even if it happens.

discrete_risks.name: Firm load shedding in a major US RTO
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: PJM, ERCOT, MISO or SPP orders involuntary firm load shed (rolling blackouts) affecting 500,000 or more customers during a declared capacity or energy emergency.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Structurally the tightest since deregulation: 2,600+ GW stuck in interconnection queues, gas turbines sold out into 2029-30 with prices up 195% versus 2019, transformer lead times to five years, and data-center load compounding 15-20%/yr against a retiring thermal fleet. NERC assessments flag PJM and MISO as elevated risk. The supply-demand gap does not close until turbine and transformer bottlenecks clear around 2029-2031, so hazard rises through the late 2020s then eases. Weather is the trigger; the structural gap sets the conditional probability.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US RTO firm load shed events affecting 500k+ customers since 2000 - ERCOT Feb 2021 Uri (~4.5m), SPP Feb 2021 (~1m), MISO South Feb 2021, ERCOT Feb 2011 (~1m), CAISO Aug 2020 (~490k, borderline). Roughly 3-4 qualifying events in 26 years clustered in 2 weather episodes: 8-12%/yr unconditional, which I raise for demonstrated capacity-margin erosion.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high. The 2021 experience triggered enormous winterisation investment in ERCOT and SPP, and ERCOT's margins are the best in a decade thanks to ~10 GW of grid batteries that specifically cover the evening net-peak where prior events occurred. Storage clears queues far faster than the headline queue statistics suggest. Demand-response contracts with hyperscalers are now standard in large-load interconnection agreements, meaning data centers get curtailed before firm residential load - so the risk may be transferred rather than realised. 35% by 2031 is arguable.

discrete_risks.name: Global coal demand falls 3%+ below the 2025 level
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IEA reports global coal demand (Mt or Mtce) for some calendar year at or before the stated year at least 3% below the reported 2025 level, confirming structural decline rather than noise.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Coal generation fell globally in 2025 for the first time since 2019 (China -1.5%, India -3.0%), yet total coal demand still rose 0.4% because of non-power uses and Southeast Asian growth. The mechanism is now in place: ~600 GW/yr of solar plus batteries can cover all incremental Chinese and Indian electricity demand, which is CREA's stated precondition for peaking. Working against speed: China commissioned ~80 GW of coal in 2025 and approved a record 161 GW of new/reactivated proposals, giving a young fleet with strong local incentives to run. A 3% decline by 2027 needs two consecutive sharp falls and is unlikely; by 2031 it is roughly the central case; by 2036 near-certain if the solar trend holds at all.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: multi-year declines in global coal demand since 1950 - only two (1990-1999 post-Soviet collapse, and 2014-2016 which fully reversed). Every previously declared 'peak coal' (2014, 2019, 2022) proved premature, which argues strongly for humility on timing while not disputing direction.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high. Coal demand has embarrassed forecasters for fifteen straight years. Non-power coal - steel, cement, chemicals, and increasingly coal-to-chemicals in China - is roughly a third of demand and has no near-term substitute; it can grow even as power coal falls. India explicitly plans a 46% coal capacity increase by 2030, and Indonesia and Vietnam are still building. If AI datacenter load in China is served partly by coal, or a hot dry year cuts hydro, 2027-2029 could see new records. 54% by 2031 could be 15 points too high.

discrete_risks.name: Global oil demand declines year-on-year outside recession or supply shock
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IEA Oil Market Report reports total global oil demand for a calendar year below the preceding calendar year, in a year with positive global real GDP growth above 2% and no Hormuz-class supply disruption. 2026 is excluded from resolution due to the Hormuz shock.
discrete_risks.reasoning: EV penetration is the dominant mechanism and compounding fast: global EV share 22.4% in 2026, China at ~64% of domestic new car sales, over 20m units sold in 2025, now displacing roughly 1.5-2 Mb/d of gasoline demand growth. Against it, petrochemical feedstock, aviation and shipping keep growing and are far harder to electrify, and non-OECD road demand outside China is still rising. IEA scenarios put the plateau in the late 2020s; OPEC says the 2040s. The clean-resolution requirement (positive GDP growth, no supply shock) makes near-term YES genuinely hard.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: year-on-year declines in global oil demand since 1965 - 1974-75, 1980-83, 2008-09, 2020. Four episodes in 61 years, every one caused by recession or embargo, never by structural substitution. A decline in a healthy-growth year would be unprecedented, which is why the 2027 number is low.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: genuinely uncertain in both directions. Too low: China's oil demand may already have peaked in 2023-2024 on EVs plus LNG trucking, and China supplied most global demand growth for two decades - if Chinese demand falls ~300 kb/d/yr and OECD ~200 kb/d/yr, the rest of the world must add over 500 kb/d/yr just to hold flat. Too high: petrochemical demand alone could add 3-4 Mb/d by 2036, and if EV growth in India, Africa and Latin America disappoints - which the 2025-26 slowdown in several markets suggests - 2036 could still be above 2025.

discrete_risks.name: A Western SMR delivers first commercial grid power
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A small modular reactor (nameplate under 300 MWe) in an OECD member country, excluding South Korea's existing SMART-class designs, synchronises to the grid and delivers commercial electricity, confirmed by the national regulator or IAEA PRIS.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Darlington BWRX-300 Unit 1 is the clear leader - OPG applied to the CNSC for a Licence to Operate in March 2026, consistent with a 2029-2030 first-power target. TerraPower Natrium has its NRC construction permit; X-energy/Dow Seadrift targets 2030. None can plausibly deliver power in 2026-2027. By end-2031 at least one of Darlington, Natrium or a European unit must hit within roughly 1-2 years of current schedule, which is a coin flip given nuclear's record. By 2036 the pipeline is deep enough that total failure requires a systemic problem rather than project-level slippage. China's Linglong One will likely beat everyone but is excluded by the OECD criterion.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: OECD first-of-a-kind nuclear projects and schedule slippage - Vogtle 3/4 (7 years late), Flamanville 3 (12 years), Olkiluoto 3 (13 years), Hinkley Point C (5+ and counting). Median FOAK slip is roughly 60-100% of original schedule. Applying a 70% slip to a 2029 Darlington target gives ~2032; applying it across the portfolio gives roughly 50/50 by 2031.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too low. SMRs differ structurally from the gigawatt FOAK projects generating the pessimistic base rate: BWRX-300 derives from a licensed BWR design, components are factory-fabricated and road-shippable, and Darlington is a brownfield site with an existing licensed operator and trained workforce - exactly the factors that sank Vogtle and Flamanville. Hyperscaler capital (Amazon-X-energy, Google-Kairos, Microsoft-Constellation) removes the financing risk that killed prior nuclear cycles, and 70% by 2031 is respectable. The counter-counter: NuScale's UAMPS cancellation on cost showed SMR economics are unproven, and one high-profile overrun could freeze the sector.

discrete_risks.name: European gas price returns to crisis levels
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: TTF front-month natural gas futures settle above EUR 100/MWh on any trading day.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The structural picture is the opposite of 2022: roughly 300 bcm/yr of new liquefaction arrives by 2030 (half US, 20% Qatar), US LNG exports up 10% in 2026 alone, and Asian spot LNG forecast at $9.50-9.90/MMBtu versus $12.45 in 2025. Even the Hormuz closure - which removed all Qatari LNG, about 20% of global supply, for four months - did not push TTF to EUR 100. That is a strong revealed-resilience signal: storage rules, industrial demand destruction and Norwegian/US supply now absorb very large shocks. Residual risk comes from a cold winter coinciding with a Norwegian outage plus a supply disruption, or Russian escalation against remaining infrastructure. Hazard declines through the horizon as the glut deepens.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: days with TTF above EUR 100/MWh since the contract began in 2003 - essentially zero before Sep 2021, then a concentrated ~12-month episode in 2021-22 peaking near EUR 340. One episode in 23 years, caused by the single largest gas-supply reconfiguration in European history. Post-reconfiguration the unconditional hazard is low.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: possibly too low. Europe has replaced pipeline monopoly dependence with global-market price-taking: in a world where cheap LNG revives Asian demand (the glut creating its own demand), European buyers must outbid Asia in any cold snap. The 2026 Hormuz episode also proved Qatari supply is a single-chokepoint dependency Europe cannot hedge. A cold European winter plus weak wind plus any Gulf disruption clears EUR 100 easily, and 25% by 2027 is arguable.

discrete_risks.name: Lithium carbonate price exceeds $40,000/tonne
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Battery-grade lithium carbonate, China spot (SMM or Fastmarkets assessment), exceeds $40,000/tonne on a monthly average basis.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Lithium has already moved sharply - spot up ~180% between June 2025 and Feb 2026 to ~$10.48/lb (~$23,100/t) - driven by collapsed upstream investment during the 2023-24 crash (lithium capex down ~40%) colliding with stationary-storage demand that BNEF revised up 27%. That is the classic underinvestment setup. But $40,000/t needs roughly another 75%, and lithium supply is unusually elastic: Chinese lepidolite, African spodumene (Zimbabwe, Mali) and DLE restart within 12-18 months, and the 2022 spike to ~$80,000/t fully retraced within two years. Structural rather than episodic tightness is required for a sustained monthly average.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: months with lithium carbonate above $40,000/t since the market became liquid in 2015 - roughly 15 months, all within the 2021-2023 supercycle. One episode in 11 years, about 9%/yr episode hazard, adjusted upward for the current investment shortfall and demonstrated momentum.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high. Sodium-ion is the underrated killer of this thesis - CATL and BYD have Na-ion in commercial production for stationary storage and entry EVs precisely to cap lithium's pricing power, and above roughly $25,000/t Na-ion substitution in grid storage becomes compelling, putting a soft ceiling well below $40,000. LFP chemistry also uses far less lithium per kWh than the NMC assumptions in older deficit models. The counter: lithium markets are thin and overshot 4x in a single year in 2022 when spot buyers panicked.

discrete_risks.name: Annual global solar PV installations exceed 1,000 GW
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Global solar PV capacity additions in a calendar year exceed 1,000 GWdc, as reported by BNEF, IEA or SolarPower Europe.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2025 delivered roughly 600 GW of solar out of 800 GW of total renewable additions. Reaching 1 TW/yr needs about +67%, achievable in 4-6 years at historical CAGRs but not at current ones: China's Mechanism 136 reform ended guaranteed offtake, the US OBBBA cliff will collapse American installs after 2027, and Chinese anti-involution policy is deliberately raising module prices from $0.085-0.095/W toward ~$0.12/W to restore margins. Against that: 570kt of polysilicon inventory (~300 GW of latent supply), storage co-location fixing curtailment economics, and explosive datacenter and emerging-market demand. The binding constraint has shifted from module supply to interconnection and offtake.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: annual global solar additions 2015-2025 - 51, 75, 99, 106, 118, 145, 175, 240, 445, 600, ~600 GW. Ten-year CAGR ~28%, but 2024-25 was roughly flat, the first stall in a decade. Extrapolating the ten-year CAGR gives 1 TW by 2028; extrapolating the two-year trend gives never. Truth is in between.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too low. Solar has beaten every forecast every year for fifteen years, and the IEA specifically has revised its solar projections upward more than twenty times. The 2025 stall is most likely a Chinese policy-transition artefact, and manufacturing capacity already exceeds 1 TW/yr - the physical ability to install a terawatt exists today. The counter-argument: 1 TW/yr implies enormous complementary storage, grid and curtailment-tolerance investment that is visibly not being made. Interconnection queues, not panels, now set the ceiling.

discrete_risks.name: China energy-related CO2 emissions decline three consecutive years
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IEA or CREA reports China's energy-related CO2 emissions declining year-on-year in three consecutive calendar years, with the third such year at or before the stated year.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Preconditions are visibly in place: China's coal generation fell 1.5% in 2025, clean-energy additions now exceed incremental electricity demand, and China accounted for 58% of global electricity demand growth while still cutting power-sector emissions. CREA argues coal power expansion has run out of room. But three consecutive declines is demanding - it requires no rebound year from drought-hit hydro, no stimulus-driven construction cycle, and no AI datacenter buildout served by coal. Chinese emissions have wobbled around a plateau since 2023 rather than clearly declining, and ~80 GW of coal commissioned in 2025 with 161 GW of proposals leaves a very young fleet with strong local pressure to run.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: three-consecutive-year declines in Chinese energy CO2 since 1980 - never. The 2014-2016 near-miss (two years of decline) reversed in 2017 on construction stimulus. This is genuinely unprecedented and the base rate is essentially zero, which anchors the 2027 number very low.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: uncertain, differing by horizon. Too high on 2027: Chinese emissions data are revised heavily and late - the National Bureau of Statistics restates energy balances by several percent, so three consecutive declines may not be identifiable until years afterward and may be revised away entirely. Too low on 2031: the 15th Five-Year Plan is expected to set an absolute carbon cap, and once a binding cap exists the CCP delivers on it - Chinese five-year targets are met far more reliably than Western ones, which would make sustained decline near-automatic.

discrete_risks.name: LME copper exceeds $15,000/tonne
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: LME 3-month copper settles above $15,000/tonne (nominal USD) on a monthly average basis.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Copper has the most genuinely structural deficit thesis of any material: grid buildout, datacenter power distribution, EVs and renewables all demand copper simultaneously while grades decline, permitting takes 15+ years, and Chilean/Peruvian output disappoints. Base metals rose about a third between January 2025 and April 2026 with copper at record highs, and copper-focused capex rose 8% while lithium capex fell 40% - the market believes the story. But $15,000/t is roughly 30-40% above current record levels; copper demand is price-elastic through aluminium substitution in cables, transformers and busbars, and scrap responds strongly at high prices. The deficit widens through the late 2020s as grid investment peaks, hence the rising profile.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: real-terms copper price episodes since 1900 - copper has exceeded roughly 2x its long-run real average three or four times (1970s, 2006-08, 2011, arguably 2024-26). Roughly 4 episodes in 125 years for a doubling-scale move, though frequency has increased since 2000. Nominal thresholds also erode: $15,000 in 2036 is about $11,800 in today's money.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too high. Aluminium substitution is chronically underrated by copper bulls - utility distribution cable, transformer windings and some motor windings can and do switch to aluminium at sustained high copper prices, and Chinese grid operators have already standardised on aluminium alloy for much distribution. Copper's 'no substitute' framing is marketing, not physics. The grid buildout driving the deficit is itself constrained by transformers and permitting rather than copper, so if grid investment is throttled elsewhere copper demand disappoints. The counter: if the AI datacenter buildout approaches announced scale, every copper demand estimate is too low.

discrete_risks.name: Coordinated physical attack causes a major OECD outage
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A deliberate physical attack (sabotage, arson, gunfire, explosive) causes loss of electricity supply to 500,000 or more customers for 24 or more hours in an OECD member country, confirmed as deliberate by law enforcement.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Attack frequency is clearly rising - the 3 Jan 2026 Berlin cable-bridge arson cut power to 40,000 households and 2,000 businesses in Berlin's longest outage since 1945; US substation attacks (Moore County NC 2022, ~45,000 customers for 4 days) are now routine enough that NERC tracks them separately; Nord Stream and Baltic cable incidents normalised state-deniable infrastructure sabotage. But the severity threshold here is an order of magnitude above anything achieved: 500,000 customers for 24 hours requires either simultaneous multi-substation coordination with real engineering knowledge or an attack on a transmission chokepoint. Amateur attacks hit distribution, which is redundant.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: deliberate physical attacks on OECD electricity infrastructure causing outages 2013-2026 - Metcalf 2013 (no outage), Moore County 2022 (45k/4 days), Pacific Northwest substations 2022 (~14k), French grid and rail sabotage 2024-25, Berlin 2026 (40k/2 days). Roughly 5-8 notable events in 13 years, none exceeding ~50,000 customers. Zero at the 500k threshold: base rate under 1%/yr, raised for escalating frequency and state-actor involvement.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: too low under conflict conditions, roughly right in peacetime. Russian sabotage networks in Europe escalated from arson to rail to undersea cables in three years while grid physical security has not remotely kept pace - most substations have a chain-link fence, and the engineering knowledge is public (the 2013 FERC study identifying nine critical substations leaked). Against that: transformer sabotage causes long outages only where spares are absent, and post-2013 spare transformer reserve programmes in the US and EU specifically address this, with operators usually able to reroute within hours.

discrete_risks.name: Global installed water electrolysis capacity reaches 25 GW
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IEA Global Hydrogen Review reports cumulative installed and operating water electrolysis capacity worldwide of 25 GW or more.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is the reality-check risk framed positively. Roughly 2.5 GW is operational or under construction globally at end-Q1 2026 against an announced 2030 pipeline of ~150 GW - a 60x gap between announcement and steel in the ground. About 60 projects (~4.9 Mtpa) were cancelled in 2025 alone, including the Topsoe/First Ammonia 5 GW agreement and 1.88 GW withdrawn from the European Hydrogen Bank auction. The viability gap is fundamental: $3-6/kg production cost against grey hydrogen at $1-2/kg, with no offtaker willing to pay the difference absent mandates. Reaching 25 GW requires a 10x from here, essentially requiring both EU RED III mandates and the 45V credit to be enforced hard. By 2036 it becomes plausible if hard-to-abate sectors face real carbon costs.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: announced-to-delivered ratios for hydrogen since 2020 - in every year the IEA has published a Global Hydrogen Review, delivered capacity has come in at roughly 5-10% of what the pipeline implied two years earlier. Applying a 7% realisation rate to the ~150 GW 2030 pipeline gives about 10 GW by 2030, well short of 25 GW.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: probably too low. Ammonia and refining already consume ~90 Mt/yr of grey hydrogen; displacing even 5% with electrolysis is ~30 GW. If electricity in solar-rich regions reaches $10-15/MWh - which negative-price hours in Chile, Australia and the Middle East already touch - electrolytic hydrogen undercuts grey without subsidy. China is also installing electrolysers at scale that Western trackers undercount (Sinopec Kuqa and successors), with Chinese alkaline capex roughly a quarter of Western; China alone could deliver 15-20 GW by 2031 largely unnoticed.

discrete_risks.name: Nuclear accident rated INES Level 5 or above
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The IAEA International Nuclear Event Scale assigns a rating of Level 5 (accident with wider consequences) or higher to an event at a civil nuclear power reactor or spent fuel facility anywhere in the world.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Two distinct hazards. First, ordinary operating risk across a ~440-reactor fleet with rising average age, now compounded by pressure to run plants harder and longer for datacenter loads and by rapid buildout in newer nuclear states. Second and larger, war risk: Zaporizhzhia has repeatedly lost all off-site power and been shelled, and any renewed major fighting in Ukraine or a Middle East strike on a reactor site (Bushehr was reportedly within the 2025-26 conflict's target set) creates a pathway with no peacetime analogue. The expanding Chinese and Indian fleets add exposure with less transparent regulatory culture.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: INES Level 5+ events at civil power reactors - Windscale 1957 (5), Three Mile Island 1979 (5), Chernobyl 1986 (7), Fukushima 2011 (7). Four events in roughly 70 years of civil nuclear power, concentrated in the early era and in specific design and regulatory failures. The post-1990 rate is 1 event in 36 years (~2.8%/yr); adjusting down for post-Fukushima hardening and up for war risk gives roughly 2.5%/yr.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: DIRECTION: too high in peacetime, too low with war. Too high because Fukushima triggered genuinely global safety retrofits - passive cooling, bunkered generators, filtered vents, hardened spent-fuel pools - and Gen III+ designs now being built (AP1000, EPR, Hualong One) have passive safety systems making Level 5 very hard to reach even in total station blackout; forty years without a Level 5 outside Fukushima's specific tsunami scenario is real evidence. Too low because the horizon includes an unprecedented number of first-of-a-kind SMRs operated by new entrants, plus Zaporizhzhia, plus an ageing Western fleet on 60-80 year licence extensions with no operating precedent.

continuous_variables.name: Brent crude oil price
continuous_variables.notes: Evolve log-normally (annual log-sigma ~0.22) rather than arithmetically; annual_vol is given as an approximate USD-equivalent 1-sigma at the current level. Right-skewed: the downside is floored around $40-45 by shale economics and OPEC+ fiscal breakevens, while the upside tail is fat and driven by Hormuz/Gulf disruption. Regime-dependent - condition on energy_hormuz_reclosure and energy_oil_price_collapse_45. EIA July 2026 STEO has 2026 at $82 (H1 shock-inflated) and 2027 at $65.

continuous_variables.name: Annual global solar PV capacity additions
continuous_variables.notes: 2025 actual was ~600 GW (75% of 800 GW total renewables, IEA GER 2026). Growth stalled in 2024-25 after a decade of ~28% CAGR - a Chinese policy-transition artefact (Mechanism 136 ending guaranteed offtake) plus the US OBBBA cliff. Right-skewed: manufacturing capacity already exceeds 1 TW/yr, so upside is demand- and grid-limited rather than supply-limited. Downside is bounded near current levels because module costs are already below the point where solar is the cheapest new generation nearly everywhere.

continuous_variables.name: Lithium-ion battery pack price (volume-weighted, all segments)
continuous_variables.notes: BNEF: $108/kWh in 2025 (-8% y/y), China $84/kWh, North America +44% and Europe +56% versus China. 2026 projected ~$105/kWh. Learning rate ~18-20% per doubling but the doubling interval is lengthening. Lithium and cobalt price spikes are the main mechanism that could flatten or reverse the curve, so couple this negatively to energy_lithium_price_spike. Sodium-ion provides a soft ceiling on the upside.

continuous_variables.name: China share of global rare-earth separation and refining
continuous_variables.notes: IEA GCMO 2026 reports China above 90% for rare earths in aggregate supply terms; refining/separation specifically is usually put at 85-90%. Critically, the IEA finds the average top-refiner share across energy minerals ROSE to 70% in 2025 from 68% in 2020 - diversification is being announced faster than it is being built. Downward drift depends on MP Materials Mountain Pass, Lynas Malaysia/Kalgoorlie and Solvay La Rochelle actually ramping; Chinese price suppression is the main mechanism that stalls this. Skew is toward the slow-diversification (high) side.

continuous_variables.name: US data center electricity consumption
continuous_variables.notes: 183 TWh in 2024, compounding 15-20%/yr. The widest-uncertainty variable in the domain: depends on AI capex persistence, inference efficiency gains, and whether interconnection constraints bind (queues 4-7 years in NoVA/Phoenix/Dallas, turbines sold out into 2029-30). Heavily right-skewed but genuinely bimodal - an AI capex bust leaves this near 300 TWh in 2031 while a continued buildout exceeds 700. Should be modelled with a regime switch rather than pure GBM.

continuous_variables.name: EU average wholesale electricity price
continuous_variables.notes: 2025 EU wholesale average was ~USD 95/MWh (roughly EUR 88), up ~10% y/y in line with TTF. Downward drift from the LNG glut (300 bcm/yr of new liquefaction by 2030) and rising renewables share; upward pressure from network charges (+46% since 2019) and non-recoverable taxes (+15%), which do not appear in the wholesale number but drive the industrial delivered price. The wholesale figure understates the competitiveness problem: EU industrial delivered power is over 2x US and ~1.5x China largely because of network and tax components.

continuous_variables.name: Global coal demand
continuous_variables.notes: NOT VERIFIED this session - the 8,800 Mt level comes from pre-2026 IEA reporting. What I did verify: demand grew 0.4% in 2025 while generation fell (China -1.5%, India -3.0%). Non-power coal (steel, cement, coal-to-chemicals) is about a third of the total and nearly inelastic near-term, capping the rate of decline. China commissioned ~80 GW of coal in 2025 with a record 161 GW of new proposals, so a young fleet with strong local run incentives sets the downside floor. Hydro variability drives most of the year-to-year volatility.

continuous_variables.name: Uranium spot price
continuous_variables.notes: Verified at $83-85/lb in January 2026, a 17-month high. Structurally tight - Goldman models a cumulative 1.9bn lb net deficit 2025-2045, and the Kazatomprom/Cameco supply response has repeatedly disappointed. Thin, illiquid spot market with a history of violent overshoots ($136 in 2007, $107 in 2024). Right-skewed. Couple to datacenter-driven nuclear PPA demand and to energy_western_smr_first_power. HALEU is a separate and tighter chokepoint not captured by this variable.

continuous_variables.name: Global oil (liquids) demand
continuous_variables.notes: 2026 is distorted downward by the Hormuz shock and elevated H1 prices; the pre-shock underlying trend was ~+0.8-1.1 Mb/d/yr and decelerating. Drift should decay toward zero and then negative around 2030-2033 as EV penetration compounds (global EV share 22.4% in 2026, China ~64% of domestic new car sales). Left tail is recession-driven and fat; right tail is bounded by refinery and petrochemical capacity. Petrochemical feedstock and aviation are the growth components; road gasoline is the declining one.

continuous_variables.name: Global LNG liquefaction nameplate capacity
continuous_variables.notes: The most predictable variable in the domain - capacity under construction is sanctioned, financed and physically visible, so uncertainty is commissioning-schedule slippage rather than volume. Roughly 300 bcm/yr (~220 Mtpa) of additions to 2030, about half US and 20% Qatar (North Field East/South/West). Low vol, near-certain direction. The interesting derived quantity is utilisation, not capacity: a glut means nameplate rises while utilisation falls, and utilisation is what sets TTF and JKM.

continuous_variables.name: Global EV share of new light-vehicle sales
continuous_variables.notes: Verified ~22.4% for 2026, over 20m units in 2025, China ~64% of domestic new car sales (NEV basis, includes PHEV). Growth is bifurcating: China and parts of Europe are on the steep segment of the S-curve while the US decelerates sharply after OBBBA credit removal and emerging markets are just starting. S-curve dynamics mean drift should decay as global share passes ~50%. Battery cost is the main driver - couple negatively to battery_pack_price_usd_kwh and to energy_lithium_price_spike.

continuous_variables.name: Henry Hub natural gas price
continuous_variables.notes: EIA STEO July 2026 has 2026 averaging ~$3.70 and 2027 easing below $3.50 on record production (122.4 Bcf/d marketed). Structural upward pressure from LNG export pull (US exports +10% in 2026) and gas-fired datacenter load; downward pressure from Permian associated gas and relentless Appalachian productivity gains. Right-skewed with weather-driven winter spikes. US-versus-Europe industrial competitiveness is essentially the spread between this and TTF, so model the two jointly.

feedback_loops.name: Solar and battery learning curve
feedback_loops.mechanism: Cumulative deployment drives manufacturing scale and process learning, lowering unit cost roughly 18-20% per doubling, which expands the set of economically viable applications and geographies, which drives further deployment. Currently the strongest loop in the energy system: solar added 600 TWh of generation in 2025, the largest single-year increase from any source in history, at module prices of $0.085-0.095/W. The loop is self-sustaining without subsidy in most markets, which is why the US OBBBA rollback slows but does not stop it.

feedback_loops.name: Oil price and shale capital cycle
feedback_loops.mechanism: Low prices cut shale capex and rig counts (551 rigs in May 2026, -25 y/y; Permian -12%), reducing US supply within 9-15 months given steep shale decline curves, which tightens the market and lifts prices, which restores capex. The fastest-acting balancing loop in commodities and what floors Brent around $50-55. It has weakened since 2020 because investor pressure for capital discipline dampens the upside response - shale now responds more to price falls than to price rises, an asymmetry that pushes long-run prices higher.

feedback_loops.name: Export controls drive substitution and onshoring
feedback_loops.mechanism: Chinese critical-mineral export controls spike ex-China prices (up to sixfold for some REEs) and create existential supply risk for Western manufacturers, unlocking government subsidy, price floors, offtake guarantees and defence-budget capital for non-Chinese supply (MP Materials, Lynas, Solvay) while simultaneously driving engineering substitution (ferrite and rare-earth-free motors, sodium-ion, aluminium for copper). Over 5-10 years this erodes exactly the leverage the controls exercise, which is why Beijing rations their use. Slow-acting: IEA data show the top-refiner share still rising through 2025, so the loop has not yet bitten.

feedback_loops.name: AI load growth into grid scarcity into political backlash
feedback_loops.mechanism: Datacenter demand growing 15-20%/yr collides with 2,600 GW interconnection queues, sold-out turbines (GE Vernova into 2029-30, prices +195% versus 2019) and five-year transformer lead times. Scarcity raises wholesale and capacity prices, which passes into retail bills, which generates voter backlash and state-level siting restrictions, moratoria and large-load tariffs that shift costs onto datacenters. Already visible in PJM capacity auction politics. The loop constrains the buildout without resolving the underlying shortage.

feedback_loops.name: LNG glut creates its own demand
feedback_loops.mechanism: Roughly 300 bcm/yr of new liquefaction by 2030 pushes JKM and TTF down (Asian spot forecast $9.50-9.90/MMBtu in 2026 versus $12.45 in 2025), making gas competitive against coal in South and Southeast Asia and reviving idled European industrial demand, which absorbs the surplus and re-tightens the market by the early 2030s. This is why LNG gluts historically last 3-5 years rather than a decade. It also makes cheap LNG a genuine coal-displacement mechanism in Asia, cutting against coal-decline pessimism.

feedback_loops.name: Renewables cannibalise their own market value
feedback_loops.mechanism: As solar share rises, midday prices collapse toward zero or negative, cutting the capture price of the marginal solar plant and undermining merchant project economics even as LCOE falls. This throttles deployment in high-penetration markets until storage, demand shifting or interconnection restores value. China's Mechanism 136 reform ending guaranteed offtake made this loop bite hard in 2025 and is a major reason global solar additions stalled at ~600 GW. Batteries are the loop-breaker, which is why storage deployment growth now outpaces solar growth.

feedback_loops.name: Energy security shocks accelerate domestic buildout
feedback_loops.mechanism: A supply shock (Hormuz closure, Russian gas cutoff, REE embargo) converts energy policy from a climate question into a national security question, unlocking state capital, emergency permitting and defence-adjacent financing for domestic clean generation, nuclear and mineral processing at a speed climate arguments never achieve. The 2022 Russia shock produced REPowerEU and a durable step-change in European heat pumps and solar; the 2026 Hormuz closure is likely to do the same for electrification and strategic mineral stockpiles. Perversely, shocks are the fastest transition accelerant available.

feedback_loops.name: Grid scarcity pushes load behind the meter
feedback_loops.mechanism: Multi-year interconnection queues push hyperscalers toward behind-the-meter generation - on-site gas, fuel cells, nuclear PPAs and co-located generation - which removes their load and their contribution from the regulated cost base, raising network tariffs for remaining ratepayers, which further incentivises the largest and best-capitalised remaining loads to defect. The classic utility death-spiral mechanism, now driven by hyperscalers rather than rooftop solar, and actively contested in state regulatory proceedings.

structural_uncertainties: AI compute demand could be wrong by a factor of three in either direction, and it is the single largest new driver in this model. A capex retrenchment - from inference efficiency gains, model commoditisation, or a financing shock - would remove the demand pull currently justifying gas turbine orders into 2030, uranium at 17-month highs, nuclear restarts and most of the grid-scarcity narrative. Conversely a buildout at announced scale would break the grid in several US regions and pull coal and gas retirements forward by years. Every datacenter-linked variable here is conditional on a regime that may not persist.

Chinese domestic policy is opaque and can re-price the entire global clean-tech cost curve on short notice. 'Anti-involution' consolidation is deliberately raising module prices from $0.085/W toward $0.12/W; the 15th Five-Year Plan may set an absolute carbon cap or may prioritise energy security and coal. SAMR blocking the $7bn polysilicon capacity-reduction plan on antitrust grounds in January 2026 shows even Beijing's own agencies work at cross purposes. Nearly all cost-curve extrapolations here implicitly assume Chinese overcapacity persists; successful consolidation would raise global clean-energy costs 20-40% and make deployment forecasts too high.

Energy statistics are revised heavily and late, so several 'peak' propositions in this model may be unresolvable or resolved differently in retrospect. China's National Bureau of Statistics restates energy balances by several percent; the IEA revises global oil demand history by hundreds of kb/d; datacenter consumption has no consistent measurement standard and estimates for the same year vary by 2x across sources. Any risk defined on 'peak' or 'consecutive decline' carries resolution ambiguity the probability estimates do not capture.

Substitution could vaporise the critical-minerals chokepoint far faster than any supply-side diversification. Sodium-ion for stationary storage and entry EVs, LFP displacing NMC (already dominant), ferrite and rare-earth-free motors, and aluminium replacing copper in distribution and transformers are all commercially available today and become compelling at price levels this model treats as reachable. If two or three scale simultaneously, Chinese refining dominance becomes strategically irrelevant within a decade and half the risks in this domain evaporate. The model treats mineral demand as roughly technology-fixed, which is a known weakness.

The Gulf security order could reconfigure entirely. The 2026 Hormuz closure was a regime-defining event whose aftermath - Iranian internal stability, durability of the 60-day truce, the nuclear programme, Saudi-Iranian normalisation, and Chinese willingness to underwrite Gulf security - is genuinely open. A durable US-Iran settlement with sanctions relief would add 1-2 Mb/d to an already oversupplied market and collapse the geopolitical risk premium; Iranian regime collapse or a wider regional war would do the opposite. Oil and gas prices here are conditioned on a status quo with roughly a 50% chance of not holding.

A technology discontinuity outside the model's frame could invalidate its cost and constraint structure: commercially viable enhanced geothermal at scale (firm clean power without the grid buildout), grid-enhancing technologies and advanced conductors that unlock existing transmission without new lines, long-duration storage that breaks the renewables cannibalisation loop, or a fusion milestone that redirects capital allocation before delivering electrons. The model assumes the 2026 technology set with incremental learning, which has been wrong about solar and batteries in every prior decade.

Physical climate shocks are treated exogenously here but interact strongly with energy: drought cuts hydro (the largest driver of year-to-year coal demand variance, repeatedly forcing Chinese and Brazilian coal and gas surges), heat cuts thermal and nuclear efficiency and cooling-water availability while spiking peak demand, and extreme weather triggers essentially every historical firm-load-shed event. A single severe El Nino or European drought year would move several variables simultaneously in the same direction, which a model with independent stochastic drivers systematically under-weights.

Sanctions and trade-regime discontinuity: roughly 5 Mb/d of Russian crude plus large volumes of Russian LNG, uranium and enrichment services move under an architecture that could either unwind rapidly (Ukraine settlement) or tighten sharply (secondary sanctions on Chinese and Indian buyers). Russia supplies a material share of global enrichment capacity, so a hard cutoff would hit the nuclear expansion assumptions directly. This model has no explicit Russia node, a significant omission given its share of oil, gas, uranium and enrichment.

research.state_of_play:
The defining H1-2026 event, which I verified by search and which post-dates my training, is a large Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) epidemic in eastern DRC. DRC and Uganda declared the outbreak on 15 May 2026; WHO's Director-General determined it a PHEIC on 17 May 2026 (first IHR Emergency Committee 19 May). As of data through 26 July 2026, DRC reported 3,262 confirmed cases and 1,437 deaths (Ituri 2,901/1,207 across 28 of 36 health zones; North Kivu 314/204). Uganda had 20 cases/2 deaths and has been cleared; one case reached France, and a US aid worker was medevaced to Germany on 13 July. This is already the largest BDBV outbreak ever and, by growth rate, the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — approaching the 3,470-case Kivu 2018-20 total in ~10 weeks rather than 23 months. The decisive difference: there is no licensed vaccine or therapeutic for Bundibugyo (Ervebo and mAbs are Zaire-specific), so the ring-vaccination tool that contained 2018-20 is unavailable. Oxford's ChAdOx1-BDBV enrolled its first volunteer 24 July 2026 and CEPI has committed >$60M across three candidates, but none will reach this outbreak. WHO's $115M appeal is ~40% funded. Reported declines in *suspected* cases appear to reflect surveillance/testing collapse rather than epidemiological retreat — a measurement caveat I flag strongly.

H5 avian influenza remains a slow-burn panzootic, not an acute crisis. Globally only 12 human A(H5N1) cases (3 deaths; Bangladesh, Cambodia, India) were reported 4 Aug 2025–10 Jun 2026; cumulative 1997-2026 is 1,022. US human cases total 71 since 2024 with 2 deaths — human infections have sharply decelerated from the 2024 dairy-worker surge. The world's first-ever human H5N5 case (Grays Harbor County, WA; confirmed 13 Nov 2025, died 21 Nov 2025) produced no secondary transmission. Animal-side, however, the reservoir keeps expanding: 1,166+ US dairy herds across 19 states as of 22 July 2026 (Idaho leads with 173), poultry detections in 12 states in June 2026, and D1.1/D1.2 genotype spillovers into cattle and swine alongside dominant B3.13. CDC's IRAT keeps recent 2.3.4.4b isolates at "moderate," public risk "low." Countermeasure capacity moved backwards: HHS terminated 22 BARDA mRNA projects (~$500M) in Aug 2025 including the $766M Moderna H5N1 award.

US public health institutions are in visible disarray. CDC's workforce is down roughly a third in about a year; the agency has had no Senate-confirmed director since Monarez's removal (Aug 2025), with acting director O'Neill and deputy Abraham both gone by late Feb 2026. ACIP was reconstituted and narrowed COVID, MMRV (split under age 4) and hepatitis B (birth dose moved to shared clinical decision-making) recommendations; a D. Mass. court stay on 16 March 2026 postponed the revised 2026 childhood schedule, largely reverting to January 2025 versions, and AAP now publishes a competing schedule. Congress rejected the proposed 53% CDC / 40% NIH cuts — the FY2026 Labor-HHS bill signed 3 Feb 2026 gave CDC $9.2B (flat) and NIH ~$48.7-49B (+$415M). Consequences are showing in measles: 2,295 confirmed US cases as of 22 July 2026, the most since 1991, with genomic evidence (lineage D8-9171) of unbroken domestic transmission since January 2025. PAHO's Regional Verification Commission reviews US elimination status in November 2026.

Global architecture is weaker. US withdrawal from WHO took effect January 2026; WHO cut its 2026-27 programme budget from $5.3B to $4.2B and still faces roughly a $1.7B gap. Amended IHR entered into force 19 Sept 2025 with 11 rejections including the US. The Pandemic Agreement (adopted May 2025) is stalled pending its PABS annex — IGWG7 concluded July 2026 without agreement, IGWG8 runs 14-18 Sept 2026, and the outcome is slated for WHA80 (May 2027) or an earlier special session. Financing: Gavi 6.0 raised >$9B against $11.9B; Global Fund GC8 ~$11B against $18B; international HIV financing fell 18% to $7.3B in 2025. UNAIDS (27 July 2026) reported 1.2M new HIV infections and 570,000 AIDS deaths in 2025 — record lows, but described as "extremely fragile." Malaria deaths rose to 610,000 (2024); TB killed 1.23M (2024). WUENIC (15 July 2026) put 2025 DTP3 at 85% and zero-dose children at 13.5M. Respiratory season 2025-26 was an H3N2 subclade-K drift year (~11M US illnesses, 120k hospitalizations, 5,000 deaths by early Jan 2026; European VE 25-45%); COVID is quiescent with NB.1.8.1 dominant and ~1,200 US weekly admissions in mid-July 2026. GLP-1 use hit 12.4% of US adults (June 2026) and Gallup-measured obesity fell to 36.4% from a 39.9% peak. I could NOT verify current Metaculus/Polymarket H5 pandemic odds, current 2026 Lassa/Oropouche figures, or post-March 2026 CDC leadership resolution.
